verified_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Lanka Kand doha 63, chaupai 4 (Manas Piyush half-lines 7-8), Gita Press numbering. Our id/ref_label say doha 62: off by one against Gita Press / Manas Piyush.
attribution_note: Kumbhakarna to Vibhishan on the battlefield, as stated. Setting is right: Vibhishan has just told him of being kicked out by Ravana and taking refuge with Ram.
translation_note: Our Awadhi text drops a word: the standard reading is 'सुनु सुत भयउ कालबस रावन' (Manas Piyush prints 'सुत'). Our English already says 'Listen, son', so only the sanskrit field needs fixing. Manas Piyush explains 'सुत' as affection: an elder brother speaks to a younger like a father to a son. Our 'line' says 'brother', which is also how Growse renders it, so that is fine. Manas Piyush notes a variant reading 'दिनकर कुल भूषन' (Manas Mayank) but rejects it; 'निसिचर कुल भूषन' is the accepted reading.
context: Kumbhakarna has been woken to fight. He has already told Ravana that abducting Sita was wrong, yet he goes out to fight for him. Vibhishan, now on Ram's side, comes forward and touches his feet, explaining that Ravana kicked him out for giving good advice. Kumbhakarna embraces him and praises him. In the doha that follows he tells Vibhishan to worship Ram without guile and to go, because he himself is 'in death's grip' and can no longer tell his own side from the other.

key_terms.sense: in the power of Time/death: so set on ruin that no counsel can reach him
the best possible advice, the highest counsel
blessed, blessed, thrice blessed: a triple, emphatic praise
ornament of the night-roamers' (rakshasa) line; the one who brings honour to the family

core_teaching: A man who has himself chosen loyalty to a doomed brother still sees clearly that the brother who left to follow the right is the true honour of the family, and blesses him rather than calling him a traitor.

commentaries.gist: 'Son' shows Kumbhakarna's fatherly tenderness for a younger brother; the Adhyatma Ramayana also has him say 'vatsa'. Being 'in Time's grip' and deaf to advice is said of Ravana by Mandodari, Prahasta, Vibhishan and Valmiki's Maricha too.

commentaries.who: Ramayan Parichaya, Ramayan Pradip and Manas Mayank, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: Three 'blessed's mean blessed in all three times and worlds. Or: Vibhishan is the third brother. Or: his mother, his father and he himself are all blessed, or he is blessed in thought, word and deed.

commentaries.who: Manas Piyush note on Valmiki contrast
commentaries.gist: Valmiki's Ravana called Vibhishan the disgrace of the clan (kulapamsana). Here Kumbhakarna overturns that by calling him its ornament, and it clears the guilt Vibhishan felt about meeting his brother.
Read 'nisichar' and 'kul-bhushan' separately: though a rakshasa, you have honoured Pulastya's line, which the rest of us disgraced.

practical_reading: Teachers use the scene for families split by conviction: you can disagree with a sibling's choice, even stay on the other side, and still honour them for following their conscience. It also notes how someone set on ruin cannot hear good advice.
misreadings: Not an endorsement of Kumbhakarna's choice to fight for a cause he knows is wrong; the poem presents that as his being 'in death's grip'.
Not a call to abandon family whenever you disagree; Vibhishan first gave counsel and was thrown out.
cautions: Kumbhakarna goes on to say he is doomed and about to die; for someone estranged from a sibling who is ill or dying the scene can be heavy.
Calls Ravana's state 'in the grip of death'; avoid implying that a stubborn relative is beyond hope.
speaks_to: siblings or relatives who chose different sides
someone who left a family business, faith or path on principle and fears being seen as a traitor
blessing someone even when you can't follow them
giving advice to someone who will not listen
not_for: someone currently being pressured to cut off family
a reader grieving a sibling they were estranged from, without framing
research_note: Read Manas Piyush vol. 6 (archive.org OCR) at Lanka doha 63 and Growse's translation (6th ed.) for the passage.

verified_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Lanka Kand doha 77, chaupai 1 (Manas Piyush half-lines 1-2), Gita Press numbering. Our ref says 76: off by one.
attribution_note: Narrator's (Tulsidas's) remark, as stated. Context: after Meghnad's death Ravana consoles his wailing wives with talk of the world's impermanence.
translation_note: Accurate. 'Sermons on knowledge' = jnana-upadesha (that the world passes, all die). Manas Piyush records a variant 'भावन' for 'पावन' (Nagari Pracharini Sabha). With that reading the line becomes 'bad things pleased him'. The usual reading is 'पावन'.
context: Meghnad, Ravana's son, has just been killed and the women of the palace are lamenting. Ravana lectures them that everything is perishable and even great demons fell to Time, while he himself behaves as if he were immortal. Tulsidas steps in with the general remark. The night ends and Ravana rides out to his last battles.

key_terms.sense: teaching about knowledge: here, talk of the world's impermanence
he himself was base, dull, wicked
those who practise it, live it

core_teaching: Fine words about wisdom cost nothing; living by them is rare. Ravana preaching detachment while clinging to his pride is the example.

commentaries.gist: Ravana tells his wives everything dies, citing Madhu-Kaitabha, Hiranyakashipu and others, yet in his pride he thinks himself immortal. That is why the poet calls him 'manda'.

commentaries.who: Manas Piyush, citing Subhashita Ratna Bhandagara
commentaries.gist: Parallel Sanskrit maxims: many are clever at advising others, but one who rises above his own nature is rare even among thousands. Preaching is easy, keeping to one's own dharma belongs to a great soul.
Wise counsel coming from a base mind is an effect contrary to its cause. He names the figure of speech: the fifth kind of vibhavana.

practical_reading: Teachers use it against hypocrisy and as a check on oneself: before advising someone in grief, ask whether you live what you are saying. It also warns that consoling words from someone who caused the loss can ring hollow.
misreadings: Not a reason to dismiss all advice because the adviser is imperfect; the content Ravana spoke is called 'pure'.
Not a blanket cynicism about teachers.
cautions: The setting is a mother's and wives' grief over a son killed in war; Ravana's 'all must die' talk is shown as empty. Don't pair it with a reader's fresh bereavement as if their grief were being lectured.
speaks_to: noticing the gap between what one says and does
being lectured by someone who doesn't practise it
someone who gives advice for a living (teachers, parents, managers)
not_for: someone already crushed by self-criticism
a grieving reader who might feel their mourning is being judged
research_note: Manas Piyush vol. 6 read at Lanka doha 77.

verified_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Lanka Kand doha 115 (ka), Gita Press / Manas Piyush numbering. Our ref says 110: off by five.
attribution_note: Ram to Vibhishan, as stated.
translation_note: Accurate. 'Nimisha' (an eye-blink) and 'kalpa' (a cosmic age) are the measures; 'each moment feels like an age' is fair. Manas Piyush reads 'सत्य बचन' as either 'my word is true' or 'hear my true word'. The companion doha 115 (kha) adds that Bharat, in ascetic dress and wasted in body, is repeating Ram's name without pause.
context: After Ravana's death Vibhishan, now king, begs Ram to stay a while, bathe, and see his treasury and palace, and to let him give gifts to the monkeys. Ram answers that all of it is his already. He cannot linger because Bharat is waiting. Next he asks for the quickest way home. The doha after says that if the fourteen years run out he will not find his brother alive.

key_terms.sense: your treasury and house are all mine: what is a friend's is one's own
Bharat's condition: his ascetic waiting in Nandigram
an eye-blink feels like an aeon

core_teaching: Ram turns down a friend's lavish hospitality without hurting him, by making the friend's wealth his own, and shows that a loved one's suffering at home outweighs every comfort on offer.

commentaries.gist: 'Your treasury and house are mine' answers Vibhishan's offer of wealth and shows a friend's dharma: treat a friend's goods as your own. Vibhishan called himself a servant; Ram calls him brother and friend.

commentaries.who: Manas Piyush, citing Padma Purana and Adhyatma Ramayana
commentaries.gist: Bharat's state: matted hair, bark cloth, living in a pit at Nandigram, barely eating, blaming himself for Ram's exile. The Adhyatma Ramayana has Ram picture him the same way, but the Manas's 'constantly repeating my name' is more intense.

practical_reading: A model for saying no to generous hospitality without offending: honour the offer and give the real reason. Teachers also apply it to how the thought of someone waiting at home makes even small delays feel long.
misreadings: Not a rejection of Vibhishan's friendship; Ram calls him brother and friend in the same breath.
cautions: The next doha links the deadline to Bharat's possible death; mild.
speaks_to: being torn between a host's kindness and the pull of home
someone far from home after a long, hard stretch (deployment, a project, hospital)
not_for: someone who cannot go home and blames themselves for it
research_note: Manas Piyush vol. 6 read at Lanka doha 115.

verified_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Lanka Kand doha 116 (first of the two-doha pair numbered 116), Gita Press / Manas Piyush. Our ref says 111: off by five.
attribution_note: Narrator (Tulsidas, within Shiva's telling). Setting right: Vibhishan rains jewels and clothes from the sky, the monkeys put jewels in their mouths, and Ram, Sita and Lakshman laugh.
translation_note: Accurate. Manas Piyush records a variant reading of the first half: 'ध्यान न पावहिं जाहि मुनि'.
context: Vibhishan has flown up in the Pushpak and is showering jewels and clothes on the monkeys, who grab them and even try to eat the gems. Ram laughs with Sita and Lakshman. Tulsidas marvels that the God sages cannot reach is joking with monkeys, and Shiva gives the reason in the next doha.

key_terms.sense: 'not this, not this': the Upanishadic way of pointing to Brahman by denying every limited description (Brihadaranyaka 4.4.22)

core_teaching: The God whom sages cannot reach and scripture can only describe by negation becomes playful and close to simple, unsophisticated companions.

commentaries.who: Manas Piyush compiler's note, citing Bhagavata 10.87.41 and Brihadaranyaka 4.4.22
commentaries.gist: 'Neti neti': the Vedas can only point at him by denying everything finite, since even he cannot reach his own end. The contrast is deliberate: unreachable for sages and scripture, easy for foolish monkeys.

commentaries.who: Manas Piyush note, with the parallel from Ayodhya Kand 136
commentaries.gist: The same idea appears at Chitrakoot, where the Lord listens to Bhil tribals like a father to his children. Only love is dear to Ram, and Shiva explains this in the next doha.
Explains why the doha's rhyme seems not to close: the joke is one-sided, since the monkeys do not see that they are being laughed at.

practical_reading: Used to say that the highest is not distant or stiff. Teachers apply it to ease and laughter in close relationships, and to the idea that simple people are not shut out of the sacred.
misreadings: Not mockery of the monkeys; the commentators read it as intimacy.
speaks_to: feeling too simple or unlearned for spirituality
joy and play after a long struggle
not_for: someone in acute grief, where playfulness may feel out of place
research_note: Manas Piyush vol. 6 read at Lanka doha 116.

verified_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Lanka Kand doha 116 (second half of the pair; Manas Piyush prints both under ॥116॥). Our ref says 111: off by five.
attribution_note: Shiva to Uma (Parvati), as stated.
translation_note: Accurate. Manas Piyush notes that 'तसि' (to that degree) implies Ram does show grace through yoga and the rest, just not as much as through love.
context: This follows the previous doha: Tulsidas has just said the God beyond the sages' meditation is joking with monkeys. Shiva supplies the reason: not practices but pure love draws Ram's grace. The scene then moves on to Ram addressing the monkeys before leaving Lanka.

key_terms.sense: love and nothing else: pure, unmixed, artless love

core_teaching: Disciplines and rituals have their place, but none draws grace as fully as simple, wholehearted love.

commentaries.gist: 'Tasi' means practices do earn some grace: after long effort the Lord sometimes appears in a sage's meditation. Love earns the special kind. The lesson: don't get lost in technique, love the Lord.

commentaries.who: Kharra (anonymous manuscript note), in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: Love has no pride in it, while yoga, sacrifice and charity keep a sense of 'I am the doer'. That is why love draws more grace.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ram Vallabhasharan, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: 'Nishkeval prem' is innocent, intense love that needs no technique at all, whether or not practices are present.

practical_reading: Teachers use it to lift the pressure of 'doing it right': sincere affection and attention count for more than perfect ritual. It can reassure people who feel they lack discipline.
misreadings: Not a dismissal of discipline or ethics; the commentary says practices also bring grace, only less.
Not a claim that love is a technique to extract favours.
cautions: Devotional framing; secular readers may need 'love' read broadly.
not_for: someone who wants a structured practice and would hear this as 'don't bother'
research_note: Manas Piyush vol. 6 read at Lanka doha 116.

verified_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Lanka Kand doha 117, chaupai 3 (Manas Piyush half-lines 5-6), Gita Press numbering. Our ref says 112: off by five.
attribution_note: Ram to the monkeys and bears, as stated; the second half is narration.
translation_note: Accurate. Manas Piyush notes a variant 'डरेहु' for 'डरपहु' (Kashiraj edition); the sense is unchanged.
context: Just before this Ram looks at them all with kindness and tells them it was by their strength that he killed Ravana and crowned Vibhishan. Now he sends them home. They are overwhelmed and say that hearing such words gives them 'moha' (they fear thinking they helped God). In the end they go with him to Ayodhya.

key_terms.sense: remember me, keep me in mind

core_teaching: After the struggle, Ram releases his companions with a parting gift: keep me in mind and you need fear no one.

commentaries.gist: 'Remember' comes before 'fear no one' because remembrance is the cause of fearlessness. Keeping his power in mind, they will never take another master. It cross-refers to 'if my servant hopes in men, what faith is that' (Uttar 46).
Their work is done. 'All of you' hints that none of them died, so they can see they have nothing to fear. Go home whichever way is easiest, and keep remembering me.
Esoteric reading: the monkeys who were portions of gods should return to their sources, while Ram's own attendants will go with him.

practical_reading: Applied to endings: when a team, a campaign or a hard season breaks up, take the bond home with you. Remembering who stood with you is a source of courage.
misreadings: Not a promise that nothing bad will happen; it is about not being ruled by fear.
speaks_to: the end of a shared ordeal or project
going home after a long time away
courage drawn from faith or from remembered support
not_for: someone afraid of a real, present danger who needs practical help, not reassurance
research_note: Manas Piyush vol. 6 read at Lanka doha 117.

verified_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Uttar Kand doha 1, chaupai 1 (Manas Piyush half-lines 1-2): the first chaupai after the opening doha, Gita Press numbering. Our id/ref say doha 3: off by two.
attribution_note: Narration of Bharat's thoughts; the second half is Bharat's own inner speech.
translation_note: Accurate. 'अवधि अधारा' can be read two ways in Manas Piyush: 'one day of the term remained' or 'one day remained of the term that was the prop of his life'. Ours combines both. The same passage tells us joy and grief rose in him together: good omens had just appeared.
context: The Uttar Kand opens on the last day of Ram's fourteen-year exile. Ayodhya is anxious, and Bharat in Nandigram has had good omens but no news. He wonders why Ram has not come and whether Ram has forgotten him as crooked. He then envies Lakshman, who was allowed to go along. Just as he is sinking, Hanuman arrives in a Brahmin's form.

key_terms.sense: the appointed term (14 years) as the prop that keeps him alive
grief without a far shore: as long as the term lasted, it had an end
crooked, deceitful: what Bharat fears Ram thinks of him

core_teaching: At the very edge of a long wait, the faithful heart turns its fear on itself: 'he hasn't come because I am unworthy.' The poem treats this self-doubt with tenderness and answers it at once with Hanuman's arrival.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ramkumar's tippani, in Manas Piyush (Gita Press)
commentaries.gist: 'Prop' means Bharat cannot live past the deadline, as he says himself a little later. Joy at the omens and grief rise in one mind together. The grief is 'shoreless' because the poet will soon call separation an ocean.

commentaries.who: Ram Shankar Sharan, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: If Ram fails to come, Bharat's oath before Kaushalya, Dasharath's praise of him and the townspeople's trust would all turn false, and Lakshman's and Guha's old suspicions would seem justified.

Bharat runs through possible reasons for the delay: Lakshman's wound, Ravana not yet dead, his own arrow that struck Hanuman, Vibhishan or Sugriva holding Ram back, shame over Sita's abduction. Finding none convincing, he blames his own crookedness.

practical_reading: Teachers read it as the voice of long waiting, which ends up blaming itself ('they've forgotten me because I'm not good enough'), and as a reminder that this fear is often untrue.
misreadings: Not evidence that Bharat really was crooked; the whole poem presents him as the purest devotee.
Not a promise that every wait ends well on the last day.
cautions: Bharat's life is tied to the deadline: he says he could not live past it, and Manas Piyush cites the Adhyatma Ramayana, where he was ready to enter fire. For a reader in despair, avoid any reading that links waiting and dying.
speaks_to: long waits for someone to come home
the last stretch of a hard period
not_for: a reader with thoughts of ending their life
someone whose person is not coming back (bereavement), unless carefully framed
research_note: Manas Piyush vol. 7 read at Uttar doha 1.

verified_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Uttar Kand doha 1 (ka), Gita Press / Manas Piyush. Our ref says doha 3: off by two.
attribution_note: Narrator, as stated.
translation_note: Accurate. 'पोत' is a boat or ship. Our note's caution (an event, not a promise) is sound.
context: This closes the opening passage of Bharat's despair on the last day of the exile. Hanuman, sent ahead by Ram (Lanka Kand), arrives in a Brahmin's form just as Bharat is going under. Bharat is overjoyed and asks who he is, and Hanuman gives him the news.

key_terms.sense: the ocean of separation from Ram
in the form of a Brahmin

core_teaching: Rescue comes as a messenger at the moment of sinking. The poem uses the image of the ocean of separation and the ship to show grace arriving in time.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ramkumar's tippani, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: The mind sinks because the sea of separation has no shore. Hanuman comes as the ship. As son of the wind he arrives at wind's speed, and he once saved Sita in the same way from her sea of separation.
For fourteen years Bharat's mind was nearly drowned. Hope of the deadline was the plank keeping him afloat, and just as that plank slipped from his hands the ship appeared.

Kaushalya had asked Ram to come back before the deadline so the 'fish' (loved ones) would survive the drying 'water' (the term). Ram did so by sending Hanuman a day early. Bharat, who loved most, was sinking first.
This answers the image at the start of Bharat's ordeal in Ayodhya Kand, where separation was an ocean and Bharat the helmsman of the ship carrying Ayodhya.

practical_reading: A picture of help arriving at the lowest point, used to say: hold on a little longer, and notice who comes. A footnote cited in Manas Piyush (Adhyatma Ramayana) has Bharat preparing to die that evening.
misreadings: Narrative of an event, not a guarantee that rescue always arrives in time.
cautions: The cited Adhyatma Ramayana parallel has Bharat preparing to enter fire if Ram does not come. Keep that detail out of readings for someone in despair.
speaks_to: being at the end of one's strength
receiving news or help just in time
not_for: someone whose rescue did not come (loss, failed waiting), where it can sound like a reproach
research_note: Manas Piyush vol. 7 read at Uttar doha 1.

verified_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Uttar Kand doha 2, chaupais 6-7 (Manas Piyush half-lines 11-14), Gita Press numbering. Our id says doha 4 chaupai 6: off by two, and the text spans two Gita Press chaupais.
attribution_note: Bharat to Hanuman, as stated.
translation_note: One error. 'बार बार बूझी कुसलाता' means Bharat asked Hanuman again and again about everyone's welfare. Manas Piyush explains this as love, or asking after Ram, Sita, Lakshman and the army one by one. Our 'He asked again and again after everyone's welfare' reads as if Ram had asked, and it sits awkwardly inside Bharat's quoted speech. Suggest: 'Again and again he asked after everyone's welfare, then said: Brother, what can I give you?' Manas Piyush also records a minority reading of 'मिले आजु मोहि राम पिरीते' (Pande ji, Baijnath): 'you, Ram's beloved, have met me today'.
context: Hanuman, in a Brahmin's form, has told Bharat that Ram is safe and on his way. Bharat embraces him, and tears flow. These lines are his response. He then asks Hanuman to tell him Ram's story, and next asks whether Ram ever remembers him.

key_terms.sense: free of debt; 'नाहिन उरिन' = I can never repay

core_teaching: Good news brought at the right moment is a gift beyond any return, and meeting the messenger feels like meeting the beloved.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ramkumar's tippani, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: Meeting Hanuman feels like meeting Ram, so all sorrow ends: meeting a holy person gives the joy of meeting the Lord. 'What can I give you' means nothing in the world matches this news.

commentaries.who: Manas Piyush note, citing the Adhyatma Ramayana
commentaries.gist: Parallel: Bharat embraces Maruti, who brings welcome words, and bathes him in tears of joy. Ram once told Hanuman the same, that he could never repay him.
'All sorrows' are the near-delirious laments of the passage just before (why hasn't he come, Lakshman is lucky). Here they are said to be gone in Bharat's own voice.

practical_reading: Teachers use it for gratitude toward people who bring relief: say plainly that you can't repay them, and let them know what their news meant.
misreadings: Not literally 'Hanuman is Ram'; it describes how the messenger's presence felt.
speaks_to: gratitude to a messenger or helper
not_for: someone still waiting with no news
research_note: Manas Piyush vol. 7 read at Uttar doha 2.

verified_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Uttar Kand doha 2, chaupai 8 (Manas Piyush half-lines 15-16), Gita Press numbering. Our id says doha 4: off by two.
attribution_note: First half narration, second half Bharat to Hanuman, as stated.
translation_note: Accurate.
context: Bharat has said he can never repay Hanuman and asked to hear Ram's deeds. Hanuman bows and tells the whole story. Bharat's one question in response is whether Ram ever remembers him as his servant. In the doha that follows Hanuman tells him he is dear to Ram as life, and Bharat embraces him again and again.

key_terms.sense: bowing his head at Bharat's feet
the story of Ram's virtues and deeds
as a master remembers his servant

core_teaching: After hearing of all Ram's glory, Bharat wants to know only one thing: whether he himself is remembered. It is the humblest and most human question in the scene.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ramkumar's tippani, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: Hanuman bows because Bharat said he could never repay him: 'don't say that, I am your servant.' Ram once said the same to Hanuman, who fell at his feet then too.

Hanuman surely mentioned Ram's words to Vibhishan about Bharat ('each moment like an age'). That shows a brother's love, but Bharat worships as a servant, so it doesn't satisfy him and he asks whether Ram remembers him as a servant.
Hanuman puts his head on Bharat's feet to say that his own being is made of this devotion, and that he will tell Ram's story with love, by the power of those feet.

practical_reading: Used to name the ache of 'do they ever think of me?' when someone you love is far away or long silent, and to treat asking as honest, not needy.
misreadings: Not insecurity to be corrected; the commentators treat it as the refinement of devotion.
speaks_to: wondering whether you matter to someone far away
long-distance relationships, parents of grown children abroad
not_for: someone who has been abandoned in fact, where the answer may be no
research_note: Manas Piyush vol. 7 read at Uttar doha 2.

verified_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Uttar Kand doha 4, chaupais 2-3 (Manas Piyush half-lines 3-6), Gita Press numbering. Our id says doha 6: off by two.
attribution_note: Ram to his companions (Sugriva, Angad, Vibhishan and the others in the Pushpak), as stated.
translation_note: Accurate. Manas Piyush records a Kashiraj variant 'अवध सरिस प्रिय मोहि न सोऊ' with the same meaning.
context: The Pushpak is coming down over Ayodhya. Ram tells Angad and Vibhishan how holy and lovely the city is. These lines say it is dearer to him than Vaikuntha, and that bathing in the Sarayu brings people near him. Then the plane lands and the townspeople run out.

key_terms.sense: Vishnu's heaven; for Manas Piyush, any imperishable divine abode

core_teaching: The Lord himself says his birthplace is dearer to him than heaven, a strong statement of love for home and of the sacredness of a particular place.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ramkumar's tippani, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: Vaikuntha is famous in both scripture and the world, yet Ayodhya is dearer: Vaikuntha surpasses the three worlds and Ayodhya surpasses Vaikuntha. 'Few know this secret' marks it as a mystery.
Ram doesn't say Vaikuntha is his own realm. 'Vaikuntha' can mean any imperishable divine abode, so sects shouldn't fight over the word. Devotees of Saket may read it in their own way.

practical_reading: Used for the pull of home and roots: even with somewhere 'better' on offer, the place you come from holds you. Also for coming home after long absence.
misreadings: Not a political claim about any modern site; it is about devotion and belonging.
cautions: The Ayodhya birthplace theme is politically charged in India today; keep the reading on home and belonging, not on any dispute.
speaks_to: loving an ordinary place more than any famous one
not_for: someone who cannot go home or has lost a home (displacement), without care
research_note: Manas Piyush vol. 7 read at Uttar doha 4.

verified_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Uttar Kand doha 5, chaupai 4 (Manas Piyush half-lines 7-8), Gita Press numbering. Our id says doha 7: off by two.
attribution_note: Narration; listener blank in our data (Shiva to Parvati frames the whole narration).
translation_note: Mostly right. Manas Piyush's prose gloss reads the thrill and tears as belonging to both brothers ('(दोनोंके) श्यामल शरीर'), since Bharat too is dark-complexioned. Our 'Ram's dark body thrilled' narrows it to Ram. Grammatically it is ambiguous, so consider 'their dark bodies thrilled'. The text's 'बर करि' / 'खर करि' (Manas Piyush prints 'खर') both mean 'by force'.
context: Ram's Pushpak has landed. He has bowed to Vasishtha and the Brahmins. Bharat then grips Ram's feet and lies flat on the ground and will not be lifted. Ram pulls him up into an embrace. Shiva then says no words can describe their meeting.

key_terms.sense: lying flat on the ground (full prostration)

core_teaching: The one who blamed himself for fourteen years throws himself down as a servant, and Ram will not leave him there: he forcibly lifts him into an embrace as an equal and a brother.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ramkumar's tippani, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: Bharat won't rise because he is lost in love. Compare Hanuman at Ram's feet in Sundar Kand. When lifting fails, Ram uses force. Bharat falls as a servant and Ram lifts him as master and brother.

commentaries.who: Manas Mayank, cited in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: Bharat crossed the ocean of the deadline by leaning on Ram's sandals. Now that the feet themselves have come, how could he let go of his life's support?
The scene is human and tender (madhurya), but the poet adds an epithet of majesty to the feet ('which gods, sages, Shiva and Brahma bow to') to show how fortunate Bharat is.

practical_reading: Teachers apply it to reconciliation: when someone who blames themselves comes to you in shame, don't leave them on the floor. Lift them up and hold them.
misreadings: Not about Bharat's guilt being real; the poem holds him blameless.
speaks_to: shame and self-blame met with acceptance
not_for: someone whose reconciliation was refused
research_note: Manas Piyush vol. 7 read at Uttar doha 5.

verified_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Uttar Kand doha 5, chhand 2 (Manas Piyush 'दोहा 5, छन्द (2)'), Gita Press numbering. Our ref says 7: off by two.
attribution_note: Mixed voices: narration, then Shiva's aside to Parvati, then Bharat to Ram. Our 'Bharat → Ram' covers only the second half; a note is enough.
translation_note: Accurate. 'आरत जानि जन' is glossed in Manas Piyush as 'knowing your servant (me, or all of us) to be in distress'.
context: Directly after Ram lifts Bharat and embraces him. Ram asks how he is, and Bharat cannot answer at once. Shiva tells Parvati that this joy lies beyond words and mind. Bharat then says he is well now: Ram saw his distress and pulled him out as he drowned. Ram then embraces Shatrughna and the others.

key_terms.sense: took me by the hand (and pulled me out)

core_teaching: Some joy can't be described, only known by the one who feels it. For Bharat, 'how are you?' can only be answered as 'well now, because you came and pulled me out'.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ramkumar's tippani, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: Love chokes the throat, so words come late. The joy is beyond words (poets can't say it) and beyond mind (it can't reach it; cf. Ayodhya 241). Mind, intellect and ego dissolve in love.

commentaries.who: Ram Shankar Sharan, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: Ram knows how hard the term was for Bharat. He had said he might not find him alive, and now he sees how wasted he is. So he asks quickly, but Bharat cannot answer quickly.

commentaries.who: Vinayak Rao's tika (Vi. Ti.), in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: Compares Taittiriya Upanishad's 'from which words turn back with the mind'. Earlier Bharat's mind was tossed by doubts. Now, united with Ram after fourteen years, it is absorbed in a bliss like the yogi's.
The mind belongs to nature and keeps swinging between willing and doubting. When the soul leaves those movements behind, it touches a joy the mind can't hold.

practical_reading: Used for moments when relief or love leaves you speechless, and for the honest answer to 'how are you?' after a long ordeal: 'better now that you're here.'
cautions: Uses the image of drowning in longing; fine for reunion, but heavy for a reader still apart from someone.
not_for: someone whose loved one will not return
research_note: Manas Piyush vol. 7 read at Uttar doha 5, chhand 2.

verified_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Uttar Kand doha 6, chhand (Manas Piyush 'दोहा 6 (छन्द)'), Gita Press numbering. Our ref says 8: off by two.
attribution_note: Narration (Shiva's telling); listener blank in our data.
translation_note: Accurate. Manas Piyush specifies a newly-calved cow whose calf still lives only on milk; 'young calves' covers that. The 'milk flowing' image is applied by Pt. Ramkumar to the mothers' love too.
context: After meeting the townspeople, Ram meets his mothers. They run to him like cows hurrying home at dusk to calves left behind. He meets each of them with great love and gentle words, and the pain of separation leaves them. In the doha that follows he meets Sumitra and then Kaikeyi, who is deeply ashamed.

key_terms.sense: a milch cow, here newly calved
helpless, under another's control (the herdsman, or fate)

core_teaching: A mother's rush toward a returning child is like a cow's evening dash to her calf, and a long separation forced by circumstances ends in a tender, unhurried reunion.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ramkumar's tippani, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: Maps the figure: mothers are cows, Ram and Lakshman calves, fate the herdsman who parted them, fourteen years the day, the evening the return. Only one point is meant: running to the child in great love.

commentaries.who: Shri Nange Paramhans, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: Bharat is the herdsman who brought the mothers away from Chitrakoot by force for their protection, to the 'forest' of Ayodhya, leaving the calf Ram behind.
The simile is inverted, since the mothers come from home and Ram from the forest. He names the figure as the second kind of asangati.
Ram meets all the stepmothers first and with great love, because the dharma texts say to honour a stepmother ten times one's own mother. He loves them in thought, word and deed.

practical_reading: Used for parents and children reunited after separation forced by work, illness, migration or circumstance, and for the instinct of a parent's love.
cautions: A strong image of maternal longing; may be painful for a parent separated from a child or bereaved of one.
speaks_to: working mothers away from young children
coming home to parents after years away
not_for: a parent who has lost a child
someone estranged from their mother
research_note: Manas Piyush vol. 7 read at Uttar doha 6 (chhand).

verified_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Uttar Kand doha 8, chaupai 4 (Manas Piyush half-lines 7-8), Gita Press numbering. Our id says doha 10: off by two.
attribution_note: Ram to Vasishtha, as stated.
translation_note: Accurate. 'जन्म इन्ह हारे' is literally 'they staked/gambled away their lives (births)'. 'बेरे' is a raft or float, a little humbler than 'boats'.
context: Just before this Ram tells all his companions to bow at Vasishtha's feet and introduces Vasishtha as the family guru by whose grace the demons died. Then he introduces them to the sage as his friends. They are overwhelmed with joy. Next they meet Kaushalya, who blesses them.

key_terms.sense: rafts, floats that carry one across

core_teaching: Ram introduces those who risked everything for him as friends, not servants, and ranks them above even his own beloved brother.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ramkumar's tippani, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: Though they are servants, Ram by nature calls them friends. The monkeys come from far countries and don't know the sage, so Ram teaches them to bow. Then he introduces them through their bond with him.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ramkumar's bracketed note, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: Etiquette was to bow giving one's father's name. Ram does it for them with one word, 'friends'. That bond would win more of Vasishtha's love than any lineage could.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ram Vallabhasharan, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: What devotees don't know, the Lord teaches them, just as Shrutideva is taught in the Bhaktamal to bow to saints.

practical_reading: Used for honouring the people who carried you through a crisis: introduce them by what they did for you, and don't rank them below family out of habit.
misreadings: Not a slight on Bharat; the commentators read it as praise of the monkeys' sacrifice.
speaks_to: gratitude to friends who stood by you
not_for: someone grieving a friend who died helping them, without care
research_note: Manas Piyush vol. 7 read at Uttar doha 8.

verified_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Uttar Kand doha 10, chaupai 1 (Manas Piyush half-lines 1-2), Gita Press numbering. Our id says doha 12: off by two.
attribution_note: Shiva to Parvati ('Bhavani'), as stated.
translation_note: Accurate.
context: Ram has met all the mothers, and Kaikeyi was visibly shrinking with shame when he met her (doha 6). Before going to his own palace, he goes to hers first and puts her at ease. Then he goes home, and Vasishtha orders preparations for the coronation.

key_terms.sense: gave her great ease and happiness

core_teaching: Ram goes first to the person who wronged him and is ashamed, and lifts her shame before he goes home himself.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ramkumar's tippani, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: This shows the greatness of Ram's nature, as in Vinaya Patrika 100. Her shame pained him, so he went to her first to remove her guilt. He had seen it when he met her (doha 6).

Four reasons: her shame; fine dharma (return to where exile began, showing the boon fulfilled); Bharat had shunned her; and Ram loved Kaikeyi more than his own mother before the exile, so he shows his love undiminished.

commentaries.who: Vinayak Rao's tika, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: Quotes a Sanskrit verse for how he may have comforted her: you gave me only my own body to guard in the forest and your small son the whole earth, so your favour plainly fell on me.

practical_reading: Teachers use it for making the first move toward someone who hurt you and now can't face you. Ease their shame rather than make them earn forgiveness.
misreadings: Not a demand that victims comfort those who harmed them; Ram acts from strength, after the wrong is over and regretted.
cautions: Can feel like pressure on someone still being harmed; keep it to past wrongs and genuine remorse.
speaks_to: reconciling with a family member who wronged you and is ashamed
not_for: someone in an ongoing abusive relationship
someone not ready to forgive
research_note: Manas Piyush vol. 7 read at Uttar doha 10.

verified_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Uttar Kand doha 18, chaupai 2 (Manas Piyush half-lines 3-4), Gita Press numbering. Our id says doha 20: off by two.
attribution_note: Angad to Ram, as stated.
translation_note: Accurate. 'बिरदु' is a sworn title or vow (Ram's reputation as refuge of the refugeless).
context: After the coronation Ram sends the monkeys home with gifts. Angad stays behind and pleads. He reminds Ram that his dying father Bali put him in Ram's lap. He has nowhere to go, since Sugriva, his father's killer's ally, now rules, and he is a boy without knowledge, wisdom or strength. Ram embraces him with tears in his eyes and still sends him home with honour, and Angad goes, looking back again and again.

key_terms.sense: your sworn name as refuge of those who have no refuge
one who does good to devotees

core_teaching: A fatherless young man begs not to be sent away and asks Ram to be the father, mother and teacher he has lost. It shows complete dependence offered in trust.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ramkumar's tippani, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: Angad's epithets fit his plea: all-knowing, ocean of mercy, friend of the afflicted. Dying Bali 'put me in your lap', so Ram is now his father. 'Remember your vow': abandoning me would break your name as refuge.
He calls himself 'deen' (helpless) because his father is dead.
Behind the plea is fear of Sugriva. Angad sees no one who would look after his welfare, so he appeals to Ram as refuge of the refugeless.
Angad never says outright that Sugriva's line will rule and he is unsafe there. He says it indirectly through 'don't abandon me' (paryayokti).

practical_reading: Applied to anyone who has lost a parent and attaches deeply to a mentor or protector, and to the courage of asking plainly, 'please don't send me away.'
misreadings: Not a promise that one will never be sent away; in the story Ram lovingly sends Angad home anyway.
cautions: Mentions a father's death; Angad's father was killed by Ram himself (Kishkindha Kand). Avoid making it a lesson for a newly bereaved child about replacing a parent.
speaks_to: clinging to a mentor at a transition
not_for: someone in a dependent relationship that is harmful
a newly bereaved child, without care
research_note: Manas Piyush vol. 7 read at Uttar doha 18.

verified_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Uttar Kand doha 20, chaupai 2 (Manas Piyush half-lines 3-4), Gita Press numbering. Our id says doha 22: off by two.
attribution_note: First half Ram to Guha (Nishadraj), second half narration, as stated.
translation_note: Accurate.
context: After the monkeys have left, Ram bids farewell to Guha, chief of the Nishad boatmen at Shringaverapura, who helped him into exile. He gives him clothes and ornaments and asks him to keep his mind on Ram. Guha weeps at his feet, then goes home and tells his family about Ram's nature.
core_teaching: Ram calls a man of low caste in that society his friend and a brother equal to Bharat, and invites him to keep coming to the royal city: love that ignores rank.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ram Vallabhasharan, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: Ram says 'coming' (meeting) before 'going' (parting). He calls Guha friend and brother, words for an equal, though no one could truly be the Lord's equal. That is how the Lord honours those who love him.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ramkumar's tippani, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: Ram had already embraced Guha like Bharat (Lanka 120). Guha's joy is at being called friend and brother and invited to the city, said to no monkey. He falls at Ram's feet to say he is only a servant.
'Keep coming and going' means Guha had daily access to Ayodhya's court, hard for others. He used to bring Bharat news and had gone hunting with Ram as a boy.

practical_reading: Used against caste and class distance: call people by the bond, not the rank, and keep the door open after the crisis is over.
cautions: Manas Piyush's surrounding commentary mentions the Nishad community's 'lower' dharma (they kill animals). Keep caste language out of any reading.
speaks_to: staying in touch after a shared hard time
research_note: Manas Piyush vol. 7 read at Uttar doha 20.

verified_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Uttar Kand doha 37, chaupai 4 (Manas Piyush half-lines 7-8), Gita Press numbering. Our id says doha 39: off by two. Growse's translation places the sandalwood lines just before his 'Doha 38' (sandal on the gods' heads, axe heated and hammered), so even his numbering differs from ours.
attribution_note: Ram to Bharat, as stated. Bharat asked to hear the marks of good and bad people. Lakshman, Shatrughna and Hanuman are present.
translation_note: Accurate. 'मलय' is the Malaya (sandal) tree. Our_note's claim about the next doha (sandal goes on the gods' heads, the axe is heated and beaten) matches Manas Piyush's account of doha 37.
context: In the royal garden Bharat, after an apology for being forward, asks Ram to explain how good and bad people differ. Ram begins with this image. The doha that follows completes it: sandal is honoured on the gods' heads, while the axe is heated in fire and hammered. Then come the marks of the good (doha 38) and of the wicked (doha 39 onward).
core_teaching: A good person keeps their own nature even toward someone who harms them, like sandalwood perfuming the axe that cuts it. The next doha makes clear that each nature reaps its own reward.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ramkumar's tippani, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: The wicked insult everyone, saints included. Saints give happiness to everyone, the wicked included. Cross-refers to Sundar Kand 41: a saint's greatness is doing good even to one who does harm.

Answers the objection that the axe doesn't actually become good. The saint's forbearance may later bring the wrongdoer remorse and reform. And either way giving is the saint's work, receiving the other's.
The saint's 'own quality' is that even when robbed of everything he holds no enmity and prays for the wrongdoer's good sense. He forgives even when harmed.

commentaries.who: Nange Paramhans (and Vir Kavi), in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: The forgiving saint is honoured even by the honourable. The axe is heated and hammered: harm-doers are punished by the anger of rulers. Vir Kavi notes one is worshipped and one punished.

practical_reading: Teachers use it for not letting someone else's cruelty change who you are, and for answering harm without becoming harmful. Our misuse note (kindness is not staying within reach of the axe) is well placed.
misreadings: Not advice to stay in harm's way or keep exposing yourself to an abuser.
Not a claim that forgiveness obliges reconciliation.
Not 'if you were truly good you wouldn't mind being hurt'.
cautions: Can be heard as telling victims to endure. Pair with the existing misuse line and with the next doha, where the axe is punished.
speaks_to: being wronged and wanting to stay decent
not_for: someone currently being abused or bullied who needs to get out
someone who would read it as 'don't complain'
research_note: Manas Piyush vol. 7 read at Uttar doha 37.

verified_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Uttar Kand doha 38, chaupai 1 (Manas Piyush half-lines 1-2), Gita Press numbering. Our id says doha 40: off by two.
attribution_note: Ram to Bharat, as stated.
translation_note: Accurate. 'अभूतरिपु' is literally 'one for whom no enemy has arisen'. 'अमरष' is resentful indignation at an insult one cannot repay. Our 'rage' is close; 'resentment' is slightly more exact.
context: Right after the sandalwood-and-axe image (doha 37), Ram starts listing the marks of the good. These are the first lines. The list goes on with a soft heart, kindness to the poor, honouring others while seeking no honour, and ends at doha 38 with 'they are dear to me as life'.

key_terms.sense: not greedy or dissolute about sense pleasures

key_terms.term: पर दुख दुख सुख सुख देखे पर
key_terms.sense: sad at others' sorrow, glad at others' joy
one for whom no enemy has arisen; without enmity
having let go of greed, resentment, elation and fear

core_teaching: The first marks of a good person: not driven by pleasures, rich in character, feeling others' sorrow and joy as their own, even-minded and without enmity, free of greed, resentment, excitement and fear.

commentaries.gist: Even when pleasures come, their mind isn't snared, because they are a mine of good character. Feeling others' joys and sorrows as their own comes from equanimity, which comes from having no enemy, and that from having no pride.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ram Vallabhasharan, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: 'Others' sorrow is their sorrow' means their own troubles don't distress them, only other people's. He cites the Bhaktamal story of Kevalram, on whose body welts rose when an ox was beaten.

commentaries.who: Manas Piyush compiler's note, citing Gita 12.15 and 12.18
commentaries.gist: 'Enemyless' and 'free of elation, resentment and fear' echo the Gita's devotee who neither disturbs the world nor is disturbed by it, and stays even in honour and dishonour.

practical_reading: Teachers use 'others' sorrow as one's own, others' joy as one's own' as a test of character: can you be glad, not envious, at a friend's success?
misreadings: Not a call to feel nothing about one's own pain; commentators describe an ideal, not a rule for the hurting.
cautions: An ideal portrait; a reader who feels they fall short may hear it as judgement.
speaks_to: envy at others' success (as its antidote)
not_for: someone already overwhelmed by others' pain (compassion fatigue), without framing
research_note: Manas Piyush vol. 7 read at Uttar doha 38.

verified_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Uttar Kand doha 38, chaupai 4 (Manas Piyush half-lines 7-8) and doha 38, Gita Press numbering. Our id says doha 40: off by two.
attribution_note: Ram to Bharat, as stated.
translation_note: Accurate. 'संत संतत फुर' means 'know them always as truly good'.
context: This closes Ram's list of the marks of the good (doha 38). Immediately after (doha 39) he turns to the nature of the wicked and warns never to keep their company even by mistake.

key_terms.sense: inner calm, self-restraint, observances and right conduct
blame and praise both the same
temples of virtue, heaps of joy

core_teaching: A truly good person stays steady in self-control and right conduct, never speaks harshly, and is unmoved by praise or blame. Such people are as dear to Ram as life.

commentaries.gist: Mind the word 'all': if any of these marks is missing, the person is not yet a true saint. Up to 'ye sab lacchan' the path of withdrawal is described, and from here the path of action.
Like Ganga water, which makes whatever vessel holds it a Ganga-vessel, gold or clay, whoever has these marks is a saint, whatever family they were born in.

Ram's list covers three kinds of saint. The devotee is described up to 'dear as life like Bharat', the knower up to 'truly a saint', and the karma-yogi from 'shama dama niyama niti' to 'temples of virtue'.
Shama: gathering mind, intellect, memory and ego onto God. Dama: mastering the ten senses.

practical_reading: 'Never speak a harsh word' and 'take praise and blame alike' are applied to daily speech and to working life: let neither applause nor criticism knock you off course.
misreadings: Not a ban on honest disagreement or firm truth; 'harsh' means wounding speech.
Not an endorsement of caste or birth as the measure of goodness (Manas Mayank explicitly rejects that).
cautions: A demanding ideal; a self-critical reader may feel judged.
not_for: someone who has just been publicly shamed and needs comfort first
research_note: Manas Piyush vol. 7 read at Uttar doha 38.

verified_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Uttar Kand doha 39, chaupai 2 (Manas Piyush half-lines 3-4), Gita Press numbering. Our id says doha 41: off by two.
attribution_note: Ram to Bharat, as stated.
translation_note: Accurate. Manas Piyush adds that 'निधि' (treasure) is like money found lying on the road: gossip is the 'livelihood' of the wicked.
context: Having described the good, Ram turns to the wicked. He first warns never to keep their company even by mistake, because they ruin the innocent the way an unruly cow leads a gentle one into trouble. Then come these lines on envy and the love of gossip, followed by more marks: lust, anger, causeless enmity, and harming even those who help them.

key_terms.sense: treasure found lying on the road

core_teaching: Envy is an inner fire: it burns at others' good fortune and feeds on hearing others slandered, the exact opposite of the good person who is glad at others' joy.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ramkumar's tippani, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: The heat is 'in the heart': they may look cool outside while burning within. They are the reverse of the saint, burning at others' wealth and happy at others' misfortune.

'Wherever they hear' means they go looking for gossip. Slander is the worst sin (Uttar 121), so it is rarely voiced, and these seek it out. Gossip is their livelihood; slander found by chance is 'treasure on the road'.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ram Vallabhasharan, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: Answering 'why avoid them if I don't harm them?': their company itself brings harm, like the gentle kapila cow that gets beaten for following the raiding cow into a field.

practical_reading: Used as a mirror more than a weapon: notice the small burn at a colleague's success, and the pleasure of hearing someone criticised. It is also used for choosing company carefully.
misreadings: Not licence to label people 'khal' and write them off; teachers read it mostly as self-examination.
Not a rule against all criticism; it targets relish in running others down.
cautions: Strong judgemental language about 'the wicked'; for a reader who feels envy, frame it as a feeling to notice, not an identity.
speaks_to: gossip at work or in family groups
understanding why someone resents your success
not_for: someone already labelled or scapegoated by others
research_note: Manas Piyush vol. 7 read at Uttar doha 39.

verified_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Uttar Kand doha 41, chaupai 1 (Manas Piyush half-lines 1-2; Manas Piyush itself cross-cites it as '41.1'), Gita Press numbering. Our id says doha 43: off by two.
attribution_note: Ram to Bharat (addressed as 'bhai' and 'tat') with the brothers and Hanuman present. Our listener 'his brothers' is acceptable; 'Bharat' is more precise.
translation_note: Accurate.
context: Ram has finished describing the good and the wicked and says such people are found in the Dvapara and Kali ages. Here he sums it up in one line. He goes on to say that those who cause pain while in a human body suffer greatly in the round of births, and that the wise therefore worship him.

key_terms.sense: the good of others, doing good to others

core_teaching: All scripture comes down to this: helping others is the highest dharma, and hurting others the lowest wrong.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ramkumar's tippani, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: Sums up the two portraits: doing good marks the saint, causing pain the wicked. 'Verdict of all scriptures' echoes the saying that Vyasa's two words in eighteen Puranas are: helping others brings merit, hurting others sin.
Causing pain while in a human body, which holds the treasury of knowledge, brings the 'great' suffering of birth and death. Those without such knowledge get ordinary suffering.
'Great crowd of becoming': being born and dying again and again with no release, or being crushed by the burden of supporting a family.

practical_reading: One of the most-quoted lines of the Manas, used as a one-line ethic: before acting, ask whether it helps or hurts someone.
misreadings: Not a call to neglect oneself for others.
cautions: The following lines speak of the suffering of rebirth for those who cause pain; leave that out for readers who fear punishment.
speaks_to: guilt about having hurt someone (as a way forward)
not_for: a caregiver already sacrificing themselves to exhaustion
research_note: Manas Piyush vol. 7 read at Uttar doha 41.

verified_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Uttar Kand doha 43, chaupai 3 (Manas Piyush half-lines 5-6), Gita Press numbering. Our id says doha 45: off by two.
attribution_note: Ram to the assembled citizens, as stated.
translation_note: Accurate.
context: King Ram calls the citizens, Brahmins and gurus together. He says he speaks without any sense of ownership or royal authority: listen, and act only if it appeals to you. In these lines he adds that whoever follows his counsel is dearest, and that if he says anything wrong they should fearlessly stop him. He then teaches the value of the human body and the ease of devotion.

key_terms.sense: what is unjust, against right conduct

core_teaching: The ideal ruler invites correction: even the king's words are to be checked against what is right, and citizens should stop him without fear if he goes wrong.

commentaries.gist: Ram speaks as a fellow citizen, not king. 'Anushasan' is guidance, not a command. Those who follow it are dearest, those who don't are not unloved, and those who fearlessly stop him when he errs are dear too.

commentaries.who: Ram Shankar Sharan, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: He addresses the 'townspeople' rather than 'the assembly' because gurus and Brahmins are present, and lecturing them would be unseemly. 'Purajan' takes in everyone gracefully.

commentaries.who: Baba Jayramdas Deen (Manas Sandesh), in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: 'Without mamata' goes with his words: he has no insistence that they accept what he says just to please him. That does not mean his words will be against niti.

practical_reading: Widely used for leadership: a good leader asks to be corrected, and the people around them should feel safe saying 'this is wrong'. It applies to parents, managers and teachers.
misreadings: Not a licence for disrespect; the correction is limited to injustice.
speaks_to: building a culture where people can disagree
research_note: Manas Piyush vol. 7 read at Uttar doha 43.

verified_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Uttar Kand doha 44, chaupais 3-4 (Manas Piyush half-lines 5-8), Gita Press numbering. Our id says doha 46: off by two.
attribution_note: Ram to the citizens, as stated.
translation_note: Accurate. 'Rarely' or 'at some point' (कबहुँक) is the key word: Manas Piyush stresses that the human body is a gift of compassion, not earned. 'सुलभ करि पावा' = obtained as if easily.
context: In his address to the citizens, Ram has said the human body is hard to win, even for gods. Just before this he says the immortal soul wanders through 8.4 million forms. Here he describes the human body as a boat with everything needed to cross. Next he says that one who fails to cross with all this is ungrateful and a self-killer.

key_terms.sense: time, karma, one's nature and the three gunas: maya's 'guards'
one who loves without any reason or return

key_terms.term: नर तनु भव बारिधि कहुँ बेरो
key_terms.sense: the human body is a boat for the ocean of becoming

core_teaching: A human life is a rare gift of grace, and it comes with everything needed: the body as a boat, grace as a following wind, a true teacher at the helm. Use it.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ramkumar's tippani, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: Time, karma, gunas, nature and maya keep the soul cycling through the four kinds of birth. The soul doesn't die, but it feels the pain of each birth and death.
'Sometimes, out of compassion' doesn't mean God is usually unkind. Devotees credit every good thing to grace and every lapse to themselves.

commentaries.who: Manas Piyush compiler's note, citing Pancharatra and Gita 9.4-5
commentaries.gist: 'Sometimes' means grace can come at any point in the cycle. No one earns a human birth by karma. God is a friend 'without reason' because nothing we do can benefit him.
Other bodies only use up merit and sin and cannot break maya's ring. Only the human body can strive. So the causeless friend's gift of it is the one way out.

practical_reading: Teachers use the boat image as a call to purpose: you already have the vessel, the help and the guidance, so don't waste the voyage. It can also be gently encouraging: you were given this life for a reason.
misreadings: Not a claim that other creatures are worthless.
Not a threat; the tone is gift, not guilt.
cautions: Assumes rebirth and 8.4 million births; the next lines call those who waste it 'self-killers', a word to avoid with a reader at risk.
not_for: a reader with thoughts of self-harm, if the next lines ('self-slayer') are brought in
research_note: Manas Piyush vol. 7 read at Uttar doha 44.

verified_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Uttar Kand doha 46, chaupai 1 (Manas Piyush half-lines 1-2), Gita Press numbering. Our id says doha 48: off by two.
attribution_note: Ram to the citizens, as stated.
translation_note: Accurate.
context: Ram has told the citizens that devotion is the easy, joyful path, reached through honouring Brahmins, good company and worship of Shiva. Here he asks what labour it involves and answers: none of the hard practices, only a straight nature and contentment. Next he warns against hoping in men and describes the devotee who wins him.
core_teaching: The path of devotion needs no heroic disciplines, only honesty of heart and contentment with what comes.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ramkumar's tippani, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: Yoga means the eight-limbed discipline, sacrifice means expense and labour, fasts and austerity mean bodily hardship, and devotion needs none of these. 'Simple nature' means no guile: inside and outside alike, words and deeds alike.

commentaries.who: Manas Piyush compiler's note, citing Bhagavata 7.6.19
commentaries.gist: Prahlad tells the demon boys the same: pleasing God takes no great effort, since he is the Self of all and present everywhere.
Contentment with whatever comes follows from trust: one who remembers him simply is looked after, so be satisfied with what he gives.

practical_reading: Used to lift spiritual perfectionism: you don't need elaborate routines, just honesty, kindness and contentment.
misreadings: Not 'effort is pointless' in life generally; it is about how devotion is reached.
Contentment is not resignation to injustice or to a harmful situation.
not_for: someone whose discontent is a fair response to injustice or deprivation
research_note: Manas Piyush vol. 7 read at Uttar doha 46.

verified_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Uttar Kand doha 46, chaupai 2 (Manas Piyush half-lines 3-4), Gita Press numbering. Our id says doha 48: off by two.
attribution_note: Ram to the citizens, as stated.
translation_note: Accurate. Manas Piyush records a second reading from Karunasindhu and Baijnath: 'if he hopes as worldly men hope (for sense objects)'. 'This conduct' refers back to the simple nature and contentment of the previous line.
context: Directly follows 'what labour does devotion take?' Ram says that one who calls himself Ram's servant yet pins his hopes on people has no real trust, and that he is won by this conduct. Next comes the portrait of the person without grudges, cravings or fears.

key_terms.sense: hope placed in men (patrons, kings, people)
I am won over by this conduct

core_teaching: Trust that is real rests its final hope on God, not on human patrons. That inward reliance, more than any practice, is what wins Ram.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ramkumar's tippani, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: This explains contentment: one who leaves Ram to hope in men hasn't treated Ram even as a man, so how is he a devotee? Cites a verse: why fret over food and clothes when the world's sustainer won't neglect you?

commentaries.who: Karunasindhu and Baijnath (footnote), in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: Read 'nar' as human patrons (kings and the like), or as hoping the way worldly people hope for pleasures. Either way it cancels the trust implied by servanthood.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ramkumar's tippani on the next line
commentaries.gist: Those enslaved to hope become everyone's slaves. Those whose only hope is the Lord are his servants and dear to him (cites Vinaya Patrika).

practical_reading: Teachers apply it to over-dependence on approval, patrons or a single person: put your final weight on something steadier. Our misuse note is apt.
misreadings: Not 'never accept help'; it concerns where the heart's final reliance rests (our existing misuse note is good).
Not a reason to stop acting or to stay in a bad situation.
cautions: Can sound like a reproach to someone who has just leaned on others in a crisis.
not_for: someone who needs to be encouraged to ask for help (e.g. in depression or crisis)
research_note: Manas Piyush vol. 7 read at Uttar doha 46.

verified_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Uttar Kand doha 46, chaupai 3 (Manas Piyush half-lines 5-6), Gita Press numbering. Our id says doha 48: off by two.
attribution_note: Ram to the citizens, as stated.
translation_note: Mostly accurate. 'अनारंभ' and 'अनिकेत' have several readings in Manas Piyush. For anarambha: starts no worldly scheme, undertakes nothing for selfish results, makes no vows and plans. For aniketa: builds no house, or has no attachment to any place. Ours ('starts nothing out of craving for results, clings to no house') follows the non-renunciate reading, which Manas Piyush supports via Tilak's Gita commentary. Good.
context: Ram has said he is won by simple trust and contentment. Now he describes the devotee in detail: no grudges or quarrels, no hope or fear, every direction joyful. In the next lines this devotee loves good company, counts heaven and liberation as straw, and holds to devotion.

key_terms.sense: no lasting enmity, no quarrel (vair is in the mind, vigraha is open conflict)
not bound to a home or place

core_teaching: Someone who holds no grudges, picks no fights, and is free of both craving and fear finds every direction full of joy.

commentaries.who: Karunasindhu and Pt. Ram Vallabhasharan, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: Vair is a deep grudge held in the mind, always watching for a chance to hurt. Vigraha is an ordinary quarrel that soon passes. The devotee has neither.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ramkumar's tippani, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: Slaves of hope are everyone's slaves. One whose only hope is the Lord is his true servant. With no hope or fear from anyone, every direction becomes joy.

commentaries.who: Manas Piyush, collecting several commentators on 'anarambha aniketa'
commentaries.gist: Pandit Ramkumar: starts no worldly entanglement, builds no house. Baijnath: claims no doership, lets things happen as Hari wills. Prajnananand Swami: begins no desire-driven action. Ram Vallabhasharan: both words mean freedom from attachment.

commentaries.who: Manas Piyush, citing B. G. Tilak on Gita 12.16-19
commentaries.gist: 'Sarvarambha-parityagi' and 'aniketa' don't mean leaving home and work. They mean giving up actions done for desired fruits and having no mind trapped in house and family. This fits a householder.

practical_reading: Used as a picture of inner freedom: drop the grudge, stop the fight, loosen craving and fear, and the world opens up.
misreadings: Not a call to quit work or leave home (the commentary explicitly rejects that reading).
Not 'never stand up for yourself'.
not_for: someone currently in danger who needs fear as a signal
research_note: Manas Piyush vol. 7 read at Uttar doha 46.

verified_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Uttar Kand doha 61, chaupai 2 (Manas Piyush half-lines 3-4), Gita Press numbering. Our doha number matches here.
attribution_note: Shiva to Garuda, as Shiva recounts it to Parvati. Setting right: Garuda met Shiva on the road while Shiva was going to Kubera's.
translation_note: Accurate.
context: Garuda freed Ram from the serpent-noose in battle and then began to doubt how a God could be bound. Narada and Brahma sent him on. He comes to Shiva, who is on his way to Kubera. Shiva answers him lovingly: a passing talk can't settle such doubt, only long satsang can. He sends him to the crow-sage Kakbhushundi, where Ram's story is told every day.

key_terms.sense: the company of the good, of those who seek truth

core_teaching: Deep doubt isn't cured by a quick answer from an authority. It dissolves slowly through long time spent among good people and in hearing what is true.

commentaries.who: Ram Shankar Sharan, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: Shiva speaks with love because Garuda came humbly and with reverence, as to a guru, unlike before. 'All doubts' means getting rid of some of them would not be enough.
Seeing Garuda's humility, his standing as Hari's attendant and his great distress, Shiva teaches lovingly. This is how one should speak to and teach someone who is suffering.
Garuda is learned in the Vedas, and a scholar's doubt is not easy to remove. That is why Shiva prescribes long satsang.
Narada said the same: delusion about God does not go quickly. One must hear the Lord's story from saints for a long time. The compiler adds that the youth of today should take this lesson.

practical_reading: Used for patience with one's own questions. Doubts about faith or life rarely end in one conversation; stay in good company and keep listening.
misreadings: Not a brush-off or a refusal to engage with doubt; Shiva answers with love and sends Garuda where he can be helped.
not_for: someone who needs an urgent practical answer
research_note: Manas Piyush vol. 7 read at Uttar doha 61.

verified_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Uttar Kand doha 69, chaupai 2 (Manas Piyush half-lines 3-4; page header 'दोहा 69 (1-3)'), Gita Press numbering. Our id says doha 68 chaupai 6: both numbers differ from Gita Press.
attribution_note: Garuda to Kakbhushundi, as stated.
translation_note: Accurate.
context: Kakbhushundi has told Garuda the whole Ram story, and Garuda's doubt is gone. He says that seeing Ram's very human deeds (being bound by the serpent-noose) gave him great doubt. Now he counts that confusion as a blessing, because it brought him here. Kakbhushundi, delighted, replies that no one is untouched by delusion.

key_terms.sense: the comfort of a tree's shade

key_terms.term: सोइ भ्रम अब हित करि माना
key_terms.sense: I now count that very error as my good

core_teaching: The confusion that drove us to seek help can, looking back, be the grace that brought us to the right person. Only someone who has burned in the sun knows what shade is worth.

commentaries.gist: How is being thrown into delusion grace? Someone in a cooled room doesn't know the joy of a tree's shade, but someone scorched and sweating does. Only one in anguish over the world tastes the joy of satsang.
Only the one who has been in error knows the special joy of the company that removes it.
Ram's deeds usually show a glimpse of divinity, but where they look wholly human, as in the serpent-noose episode, even the great are confused: Uma at Sita's loss, Garuda here.
Accepting a fault as good because of what it led to is the figure 'anujna'. The shade image is drawn from direct experience ('pratyaksha pramana').

practical_reading: Teachers apply it to hard seasons in hindsight: the crisis that pushed you to a mentor, a friend or therapy can be counted as part of the gift. The verse speaks after relief has come.
misreadings: Not a claim that suffering is good in itself or should be sought.
Not something to tell someone while they are still in the heat.
cautions: 'Your pain is a blessing' lands badly on someone in the middle of pain; this is the voice of someone already relieved.
speaks_to: looking back on a crisis that led somewhere good
having been confused or lost and found guidance
not_for: someone currently suffering
fresh grief
trauma survivors who could hear it as 'it happened for a reason'
research_note: Manas Piyush vol. 7 read at Uttar doha 69.

verified_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Uttar Kand doha 70, chaupai 4 (Manas Piyush half-lines 7-8), Gita Press numbering. Our id says doha 69: off by one.
attribution_note: Kakbhushundi to Garuda, as stated.
translation_note: Accurate. Manas Piyush records a variant 'तृष्णा' for 'तृस्नाँ'.
context: Garuda has confessed his delusion and is ashamed. Kakbhushundi says that's no wonder: Narada, Shiva, Brahma and the Sanaka sages, leaders among sages and knowers of the Self, were all blinded at some point. These lines widen it to the whole world. The list goes on with pride, youth, possessiveness, envy, grief and worry (next verse) and ends: this is maya's army.

key_terms.sense: delusion, confusion about what is real
desire makes one dance (like a puppet)

core_teaching: No one is beyond delusion, desire, craving and anger, not even the greatest sages. So being caught by them is human, not a special disgrace.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ram Vallabhasharan, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: Kakbhushundi first reassures Garuda and only then teaches. Delight makes teaching take root, while scolding first leaves the listener downcast and deaf to it.

Naming Narada and the others shows all fell to delusion, e.g. Brahma at Ravana's death and in the calf-stealing episode. The list starts with moha because moha is the topic and the root of all the 'diseases'.
The four sages and four afflictions pair in order: Narada and delusion, Shiva and desire (at Mohini's form), and so on.

practical_reading: Used to take the shame out of failing: the wisest people have been blinded, driven, maddened and burned by these same forces. Self-compassion comes first, then the work.
misreadings: Not an excuse ('everyone does it, so it doesn't matter'); it reassures and then leads to the remedy (grace and devotion).
speaks_to: shame after losing one's temper or giving in to craving
not_for: someone who has harmed others and needs accountability, not reassurance
research_note: Manas Piyush vol. 7 read at Uttar doha 70.

verified_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Uttar Kand doha 71, chaupai 2 (Manas Piyush half-lines 3-4), Gita Press numbering. Our id says doha 70: off by one.
attribution_note: Kakbhushundi to Garuda, as stated.
translation_note: Accurate. 'मच्छर' is matsara: jealousy, the wish to push another down and rise oneself, which brings disgrace. Manas Piyush also has a Kashiraj variant 'मत्सर'.
context: This continues Kakbhushundi's list of what no one escapes. Just before it: the 'delirium' of the gunas, pride, the fever of youth, possessiveness. Just after: the woodworm of desires, the three cravings for children, wealth and fame, and the line 'all this is maya's family'. He then turns to what alone frees one: Ram's grace.
core_teaching: Envy, grief, anxiety and illusion touch everyone. Naming them as universal forces, not personal failures, is the first comfort.

commentaries.gist: Grief shakes everyone and loosens patience and duty. Even steady men like Janaka and Dasharath were shaken, and the townspeople, Tara and Mandodari lost all composure in their grief.

commentaries.who: Manas Piyush compiler's note on worry
commentaries.gist: Worry burns the chest day and night; the worried are dead while alive. Quotes a saying: the pyre burns the dead, anxiety the living. A snakebite may be survived, but no one escapes the serpent of worry.

commentaries.who: Ramayan Pradip and Baijnath, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: Possessiveness destroys good name, and jealousy actively brings disgrace: people say 'he has so much and is still like this'. Baijnath: fame comes from caring for the highest, and possessiveness is self-interest.

practical_reading: Used to normalise anxiety and grief: they shake everyone, the great included. Teachers pair it with the remedy the text offers next (grace, good company) rather than leave the reader in the list.
misreadings: Not a statement that grief is a failing or a sign of weak faith.
cautions: Groups grief with envy as maya's soldiers; for a mourner, stress that the point is universality, not blame.
not_for: someone in fresh grief who might hear grief called 'illusion'
research_note: Manas Piyush vol. 7 read at Uttar doha 71.

verified_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Uttar Kand doha 73, chaupais 2-3 (Manas Piyush half-lines 3-6), Gita Press numbering. Our id says doha 72 chaupai 2: off by one, and the text covers two Gita Press chaupais.
attribution_note: Kakbhushundi to Garuda, as stated.
translation_note: Accurate. 'नयन दोष' covers jaundice and eye disease (Manas Piyush: kanvar, kamala). Our setting ('how people misjudge what they see') is broadly right, but in context the lines are specifically about people who project delusion onto Ram.
context: Kakbhushundi has said that Ram's human play deludes the demonic and delights devotees, and that only dull, sense-bound people attribute delusion to the Lord. These five images show how a fault in the seer gets projected onto what is seen. The doha that follows says those sunk in lust, anger and pride, in a dark well, cannot know Ram.

key_terms.sense: liars (what the spinning children call each other)

core_teaching: What we see is coloured by our own condition. The jaundiced eye sees a yellow moon. When we judge, especially the divine, we may only be describing our own illness or motion.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ram Vallabhasharan, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: The five examples show one thing, superimposition: the world on Brahman, a role on an actor, a mere man on Ram. Jaundice changes form, the 'western sunrise' reverses place, the boat and children project qualities.

Compare Bal Kand 115: those with a dirty mirror and no eyes cannot see Ram's form. There the eyes are missing, here they are diseased, so they see wrongly. Knowledge and dispassion are the heart's eyes.
The moon is bright and not yellow, and in the same way Ram is pure and beyond delusion. Whoever has the disease sees the disease in him.

practical_reading: Widely applied to perception and projection: before judging a person or situation, check whether the 'yellow' is in your own eye, and whether you are the one moving.
misreadings: Not a dismissal of all criticism as projection.
In the text it concerns doubts about Ram; widening it to everyday perception is a teaching application.
cautions: Can be used to invalidate someone's honest perception ('you only see that because something's wrong with you').
speaks_to: seeing a situation differently after one's mood shifts
not_for: someone being gaslit or told their perception is wrong
research_note: Manas Piyush vol. 7 read at Uttar doha 73.

verified_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Uttar Kand doha 74, chaupai 3 (Manas Piyush half-lines 5-6), Gita Press numbering. Our id says doha 73: off by one.
attribution_note: Kakbhushundi to Garuda, as stated.
translation_note: Accurate. Our Awadhi begins 'नहु राम कर' and should read 'सुनहु राम कर सहज सुभाऊ'. The first syllable 'सु' is missing.
context: Kakbhushundi begins to tell how he was himself deluded when the child Ram slipped out of his grasp. Before the story he states Ram's nature: he never lets pride stay in his devotee. Next comes the image of the mother having a child's boil lanced.

key_terms.sense: root of the cycle of birth and death

core_teaching: Pride is the root of suffering, and Ram's nature is to remove it from those who love him, even if the removal hurts.

commentaries.gist: 'Sahaj subhau' is innate, not learned or practised: it is Ram's own way. Others are moved by service, but Ram shows grace to the lowly even without service (Vinaya 162, via Ramayan Pradip).

commentaries.who: Ram Shankar Sharan, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: He doesn't worry this much about the pride of those who are not his. Ravana's pride was left standing a long time. It is his own devotees he protects from it.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ram Vallabhasharan, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: Ego is the first seed of creation. 'I am a Brahmin', 'I am a shudra', 'I am wise', 'I am a devotee' are all forms of pride that keep the round of birth going.

practical_reading: Used to reframe a humbling: when life punctures our self-importance, teachers suggest it may be care, not punishment. It also shows ego as the source of much pain.
misreadings: Not a claim that every humiliation is deserved or divinely sent.
cautions: Pairs with the next verse's boil-lancing image; avoid telling someone in pain that their suffering is for their own good.
speaks_to: being humbled at work or in life
not_for: someone who has been humiliated or abused by another person
research_note: Manas Piyush vol. 7 read at Uttar doha 74.

verified_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Uttar Kand doha 74, chaupai 4 (Manas Piyush half-lines 7-8) and doha 74 (ka), Gita Press numbering. Our id says doha 73: off by one.
attribution_note: Kakbhushundi to Garuda, as stated.
translation_note: Accurate. 'चिराव' is to have it cut or lanced. 'कठिन की नाईं' means as if hard-hearted.
context: This follows directly on 'Ram never lets pride stay in his devotee'. The doha that follows says that though the child cries, the mother ignores that pain to cure the disease. Then Kakbhushundi tells how Ram cured his own pride and delusion.

key_terms.sense: exceedingly great possessive love, a parent's sense of 'mine'

core_teaching: Love sometimes allows a short, sharp pain to prevent a longer harm, as a mother has a child's boil lanced despite the child's tears. The text applies this to the removal of pride.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ram Vallabhasharan, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: Great 'mamata' is the reason: 'this one is mine, so how could I let him fall into such suffering?'
