Out of possessive love Ram can't bear to see his own suffer, so he cuts out the root, pride (compare Narada's prevented marriage). Ordinary 'mamata' is for things, more for a son; Ram's for his servant exceeds both.

In the Narada episode the image is a mother guarding a child from fire and snake (prevention); here it is lancing a boil (cure). One reading adds the Lord gives a fault's fruit at once so it doesn't pile up.

practical_reading: Teachers use it to make sense of painful correction from someone who loves us, and of loss of status or pride that later proves healing. Our existing misuse note matters.
misreadings: Not every pain is for your good (our misuse note is correct).
Never a justification for someone inflicting pain 'for your own good'.
Not 'God is punishing you'.
cautions: A Manas Piyush gloss reads it as God giving the immediate fruit of a fault; do not pass that on to a suffering reader.
The image of a crying child held down may upset parents of sick children.
speaks_to: painful correction from a parent or mentor
a humbling that later made sense
parents making hard choices for a child's health
not_for: someone in grief, illness or trauma who might hear 'this is for your good'
survivors of abuse
research_note: Manas Piyush vol. 7 read at Uttar doha 74.

verified_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Uttar Kand doha 84, chaupai 3 (Manas Piyush half-lines 5-6; page header 'दोहा 84 (5-8)'), Gita Press numbering. Our id says doha 83. Note: one Manas Piyush cross-reference elsewhere cites the line as '83.5', so numbering is not fully consistent even inside Manas Piyush.
attribution_note: Kakbhushundi to Garuda, recounting his own thought, as stated.
translation_note: Accurate. Manas Piyush reads 'भगतिहीन गुन सब सुख कैसे' (how are all virtues and joys without devotion?) where our text has 'ऐसे'; it notes both readings. The sense is the same.
context: The child Ram, pleased with the crow, offers him every boon: siddhis, wealth, liberation, knowledge, dispassion. Kakbhushundi notices that the Lord has not offered devotion. He reflects that all of it without devotion is like food without salt, and asks for unbroken, pure devotion. Ram grants it.

key_terms.sense: happiness without worship, without love of God

core_teaching: Every gift and pleasure is flat without the one thing that gives it taste. For Kakbhushundi that is devotion.

commentaries.gist: Ram offered two kinds of thing, pleasures (siddhis, liberation) and virtues (qualities rare even for sages), and Kakbhushundi weighs both against devotion. Joy without devotion doesn't last (Uttar 119: even liberation can't stay without devotion).
Only someone who doesn't know the joy of worship runs after other joys. Without it the inner burning never stops, so what use is every pleasure when there's no rest?

practical_reading: Used to ask what the 'salt' of one's own life is, the thing without which success and comfort taste flat. In the text that is devotion; teachers widen it to meaning and love.
misreadings: Not a rejection of virtues or pleasures as bad; it is about what gives them savour.
not_for: someone struggling to meet basic needs, who may hear it as dismissing material help
research_note: Manas Piyush vol. 7 read at Uttar doha 84.

verified_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Uttar Kand doha 86, chaupai 5 (Manas Piyush half-lines 9-10), Gita Press numbering. Our id says doha 85: off by one.
attribution_note: Ram (as the child Ram) to Kakbhushundi, as stated.
translation_note: Accurate. Manas Piyush reads 'असि मम बानि', where 'बानि' can mean 'my habit/nature' as well as 'my word'. Variant 'जीवन' for 'जीवहु' (Kashiraj, Panjabi ji).
context: This is part of the 'Ram Gita' the child Ram speaks to Kakbhushundi after granting him devotion. He says all creation is his and all are dear, but his devotee is dearest. Just before this he says again and again that nothing is as dear to him as a servant. Next comes the parable of the father and many sons.
core_teaching: Status counts for nothing with Ram: the creator himself without devotion is no dearer than any creature, and the lowliest being with devotion is dear as life.

commentaries.gist: Ram has now said three times that the devotee is dearest and adds 'truly' again and again, so no one takes it as mere encouragement to worship. It is doctrine, not flattery.

commentaries.who: Manas Piyush compiler's note on 'ati neech'
commentaries.gist: Even those then counted outcaste (antyaja, chandala, shvapacha) become dear as life through devotion. Caste and stage of life drop away.

practical_reading: Used against status anxiety and hierarchy: worth before the divine doesn't come from rank, learning or power.
misreadings: Not contempt for Brahma or for the learned; it ranks love above rank.
cautions: 'अति नीच' reflects caste language of its time. Render it as 'lowly' and keep caste terms out of the reading.
research_note: Manas Piyush vol. 7 read at Uttar doha 86.

verified_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Uttar Kand doha 87, chaupais 1-2 (Manas Piyush half-lines 1-4), Gita Press numbering. Our id says doha 86 chaupai 1. Our text overlaps rcm.7.86.chaupai.2: the line 'कोउ सर्बग्य धर्मरत कोई…कोउ पितु भगत…' appears in both entries.
attribution_note: Ram to Kakbhushundi, as stated.
translation_note: Accurate, but the English ends mid-sentence ('…knowing no other duty even in dreams...'). That is because the parable's conclusion sits in the overlapping next entry. Consider merging the two entries or splitting them cleanly at Gita Press chaupai boundaries.
context: Ram has said all beings are his and all dear, but the devotee dearest. Now he gives a worldly example: a father's many sons differ in gifts and character, and he loves them all equally, yet the son wholly devoted to him is dear as life, even if he is simple. 'In this way' all beings are Ram's, and the devotee is dearest.

key_terms.sense: devoted to the father in word, mind and deed

core_teaching: A parent loves every child equally, the scholar, the rich one and the brave one alike. Ram's love for all beings is the same, and wholehearted love draws it closest.

commentaries.gist: After scripture's view Ram now gives a proof from ordinary life. 'Many' sons matches the 'many' beings he will speak of. The compiler also asks why daughters are not mentioned and answers in terms of his era's gender norms.
Rejects that question: 'kumara' stands for all offspring. The point is that all beings, male, female, napunsaka, moving and unmoving, are God's children and dear to him.
Maps the sons onto scripture: Brihaspati the scholar, Pracheta the ascetic, Sanaka the knower, Kubera the rich, the daityas the brave, Harishchandra the giver, Dhruva and Prahlad the devoted sons.

practical_reading: Used for parents with very different children, and as reassurance that you don't need to be the clever or successful one to be loved.
misreadings: Not favouritism among children; equal love is stated first.
cautions: Manas Piyush's own note explains the omission of daughters with era-bound gender assumptions; don't repeat it. Use 'children'.
not_for: someone who experienced real parental favouritism, without care
research_note: Manas Piyush vol. 7 read at Uttar doha 87.

verified_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Uttar Kand doha 87, chaupais 2-3 (Manas Piyush half-lines 3-6), Gita Press numbering. Our id says doha 86 chaupai 2. It overlaps rcm.7.86.chaupai.1 by one full chaupai.
attribution_note: Ram to Kakbhushundi, as stated.
translation_note: Accurate. 'अयाना' means simple, ignorant, unskilled. Manas Piyush: the father doesn't mind his ignorance and even counts it a virtue, because 'I am his only refuge'.
context: This completes the father parable. The devoted son, though simple in every way, is as dear to his father as life, and 'in this way' all moving and unmoving beings, animals, gods, humans and demons, are Ram's children. He goes on to say that whoever worships him with body, word and mind, giving up pride and maya, is dearest.

key_terms.sense: knows no other duty even in dreams

core_teaching: The simple child whose whole heart belongs to the parent is held dearest. Wholehearted love, not achievement, is what draws Ram closest.

commentaries.gist: The devoted son described here is Kakbhushundi himself, devoted in act, word and mind and wanting nothing but devotion. 'Simple in every way' means he has none of the brothers' gifts, while they serve the father only as scripture requires.

commentaries.who: Ramayan Pradip and Ram Shankar Sharan, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: The father doesn't fret at his ignorance and even counts it a virtue. Example: Shravana, who knew no dharma but serving his parents, and whose parents died of grief at losing him.

practical_reading: Reassurance for anyone who feels ordinary or 'not clever': being wholehearted counts for more than being impressive.
misreadings: Not praise of ignorance as such; it values single-minded love.
cautions: The Shravana example in the commentary involves parents dying of grief; leave it out for bereaved readers.
speaks_to: children with learning differences and their parents
research_note: Manas Piyush vol. 7 read at Uttar doha 87.

verified_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Uttar Kand doha 87 (ka), the doha before the soratha that ends section 87, Gita Press / Manas Piyush. Our ref says 86: off by one.
attribution_note: Ram to Kakbhushundi, as stated.
translation_note: Broadly right. 'पुरुष नपुंसक नारि' is man, napunsaka (a person neither man nor woman: neuter or third gender) or woman. 'Man, woman or of any gender' is a fair modern rendering, though slightly freer than the text. Manas Piyush records a Kashiraj variant 'नारि नर'. 'सर्ब भाव' means with every kind of feeling (as mother, father, friend and so on) or single-mindedly.
context: This ends Ram's teaching to Kakbhushundi. Having said all beings are his children and the wholehearted devotee is dearest, he declares that any being at all, of any sex or kind, who worships him without guile is supremely dear. The soratha that follows tells Kakbhushundi to worship him, leaving all other hope and reliance.

key_terms.sense: with one's whole being, in every relation

core_teaching: Devotion is open to every being without exception of sex, gender, birth or species. What counts is wholeheartedness without guile.

commentaries.who: Manas Piyush compiler's note, citing Gita 9.30-32
commentaries.gist: Shudras, women, outcastes and the napunsaka were barred from Vedic rites and study, but all have full right to devotion, in which no distinction of sex or caste remains. Gita 9.32 likewise promises women, vaishyas and shudras the highest goal.

commentaries.who: Manas Piyush compiler's note, citing Vinaya Patrika 79
commentaries.gist: 'Sarvabhava' means worshipping him in every relation at once: mother, father, brother, friend, wealth, everything. Or it means exclusive devotion, as in Gita 18.62 ('sarva-bhavena').

commentaries.who: An unnamed gloss in Manas Piyush (a contrasting view)
commentaries.gist: One gloss ranks the three as fully, half and not eligible. The compiler's main note says all three are equally eligible for devotion.

practical_reading: One of the clearest statements of inclusion in the Manas: no one is shut out by gender, sex or birth. It is used to welcome LGBTQ and gender-diverse readers and anyone told they are 'not eligible'.
misreadings: Don't overstate it as a modern statement on gender identity; it says no category of being is excluded.
cautions: Old commentaries carry hierarchical views of gender and caste; one gloss in Manas Piyush ranks eligibility. Don't import those.
speaks_to: feeling excluded from religion because of gender, sexuality or caste
research_note: Manas Piyush vol. 7 read at Uttar doha 87.

verified_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Uttar Kand doha 88, chaupai 4 (Manas Piyush half-lines 7-8), Gita Press numbering. Our id says doha 87: off by one.
attribution_note: Narrated by Kakbhushundi to Garuda, as stated. The mother is Kaushalya.
translation_note: Accurate.
context: Having taught the crow and granted him devotion, the infant Ram goes back to being a baby: with teary eyes and a sulky face he looks at his mother to show he is hungry. She runs, comforts him, nurses him and sings of his deeds. The soratha that follows says Ayodhya's people are always immersed in the joy Shiva himself longs for.
core_teaching: The infinite becomes a hungry baby in his mother's lap. This plain, tender scene of a mother answering her child's need is offered as the highest bliss.

commentaries.who: Panjabi ji and Ramayan Pradip, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: He can't speak yet, so he shows hunger by look and gesture. 'Soft words' are a mother's endearments, meant to keep him from crying. 'Singing' shows her overflowing joy.

commentaries.who: Manas Piyush compiler's note, citing Gitavali
commentaries.gist: 'Lovely deeds' are his human baby play, with no hint of majesty, which is why they are called lalita. Gitavali poems show Kaushalya rocking and nursing him while gods and sages watch from behind the clouds, envious.

practical_reading: Used to honour the ordinary sacredness of caring for a baby: feeding, soothing and singing are the very joy that saints long for.
cautions: A breastfeeding image; tender for new parents, but painful for those who lost an infant or could not nurse or conceive.
not_for: someone grieving a baby or struggling with infertility
research_note: Manas Piyush vol. 7 read at Uttar doha 88.

verified_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Uttar Kand doha 89, chaupai 4 (Manas Piyush half-lines 7-8), Gita Press numbering. Our id says doha 87 chaupai 8: both numbers differ from Gita Press.
attribution_note: Kakbhushundi to Garuda, giving his 'own experience' after recounting the Ram Gita, as stated.
translation_note: Mostly right; the closing image is open to two readings. Growse (1883) renders it close to ours: devotion 'slips away like oil on water'. Manas Piyush's gloss is different: 'जल कै चिकनाई' is the slickness of water, which looks oily but has no lasting grip. Either way the point is that devotion without love has no hold. Keep ours, or use 'like the slickness of water, which does not last'. Note also that 'knowing his greatness' comes, per the line before, only through Ram's grace.
context: After recounting what Ram taught him, Kakbhushundi gives his own experience: without worshipping Hari troubles don't end, and without Ram's grace his greatness can't be known. Then comes this chain from knowing to trust to love to firm devotion. Next he gives the soratha pair: no knowledge without a guru, no rest without contentment.

key_terms.sense: the slickness of water: not lasting

core_teaching: Love grows in steps: knowing leads to trust, trust to love, and only love makes devotion firm. Without it devotion has no grip.

commentaries.gist: A causal chain (karanamala). Worship brings grace, grace reveals his greatness, knowing it brings trust, trust brings love, and love makes devotion firm. Worship is the means and devotion the goal. Sugriva goes through the same chain in Kishkindha Kand.

commentaries.who: Ram Shankar Sharan, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: Till now Kakbhushundi gave Ram's own doctrine. 'Now I tell my experience' marks the turn to what he has tested himself.
Ram's grace is recognised when one meets a truly pure saint (cf. Uttar 69).
Renders the chain as understanding, then confidence, then affection, then consistency of faith, which otherwise 'slips away like oil on water'.

practical_reading: Applied to any relationship or practice: you can't trust what you don't know, or love what you don't trust. Get to know first, and love that lasts follows.
misreadings: Not a demand for intellectual proof before faith; 'knowing' here comes through grace and experience.
research_note: Manas Piyush vol. 7 read at Uttar doha 89.

verified_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Uttar Kand doha 89: the second soratha of the pair numbered 89 (Manas Piyush prints both under ॥89॥), Gita Press numbering. Our id says '87 sortha 5', which matches neither the doha number nor Gita Press's soratha numbering. Growse's translation labels this 'Soratha 5', which may be where our 'sortha 5' label comes from.
attribution_note: Kakbhushundi to Garuda, as stated.
translation_note: Accurate. 'पचि पचि मरिअ' is an idiom: to wear oneself out straining. Manas Piyush records Kashiraj variants ('को बिश्राम', 'पचि मरै').
context: This closes Kakbhushundi's statement of his own experience, as the second soratha in a pair. The first asks whether there is knowledge without a guru, or knowledge without dispassion, or happiness without devotion. This one asks about rest without contentment. Then he urges Garuda to drop argument and doubt and worship Ram.
core_teaching: No amount of effort brings rest without contentment, just as no amount of pushing moves a boat on dry land.

commentaries.gist: 'Sahaj santosh' means no elation at what comes and no grief at what goes.

commentaries.who: Ram Balak Das, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: Contentment brings happiness ('content with what comes, loving Ram's feet'). In the image, contentment is the water and dispassion the boat.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ram Vallabhasharan, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: The two sorathas give pairs of causes: knowledge needs guru and dispassion, happiness needs devotion and contentment. Devotion is the root, and only when it brings natural contentment is there happiness.

practical_reading: Used against burnout and endless striving: rest doesn't come from more effort but from a different footing. Teachers apply it to overwork and to chasing the next achievement.
misreadings: Not a call to stop working or to accept injustice; it concerns inner rest.
not_for: someone whose discontent is a just response to deprivation
research_note: Manas Piyush vol. 7 read at Uttar doha 89.

verified_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Uttar Kand doha 99, chaupai 4 (Manas Piyush half-lines 7-8), Gita Press numbering. Our id says doha 95: off by four.
attribution_note: Kakbhushundi to Garuda, as stated, in his description of the Kali age, which he lived through in an earlier birth.
translation_note: Accurate.
context: Kakbhushundi is describing the Kali age into which he was born in an earlier life. Truth is lost, false teachers abound, and just before this guru and disciple are 'blind and deaf to each other'. The list of decay goes on: castes mixed, people sinning and suffering fear, disease, grief and separation.

key_terms.sense: does not take away his sorrow
the 'dharma' that fills the belly: only livelihood

core_teaching: A teacher's job is to relieve the student's sorrow, not to profit from them. A parent's job is to pass on more than how to earn a living. The verse describes a degraded age in which both have failed.

commentaries.who: Karunasindhu and Baijnath, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: Guru and disciple are 'blind and deaf': the disciple won't listen and clings to pleasures, and the self-interested guru takes anyone on without looking at their qualities, just to 'blow in the ear' and collect fees.

A guru should choose disciples carefully and keep them close until they mature in practice. That is removing their sorrow. Instead these gurus extract money by praise, pressure, then anger. Parents call children away from satsang lest they become mendicants.

commentaries.who: Ram Shankar Sharan and Panjabi ji, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: The guru doesn't remove the disciple's doubt, which is his real grief, and his taking of money even adds bodily hardship. Parents teach belly-filling skills from childhood rather than learning and good company.

practical_reading: Applied to teachers, coaches, gurus and parents today: are you relieving people's suffering or only collecting their fees? Are you teaching children more than how to make money?
misreadings: Not a ban on teachers being paid; the fault is taking money while ignoring the student's real need.
Not contempt for earning a living; it criticises teaching only that.
cautions: 'Falls into a terrible hell' is punitive language; a reader hurt by an exploitative guru may welcome it, but a teacher who feels inadequate may be crushed by it.
speaks_to: people disillusioned by exploitative gurus or institutions
teachers and mentors checking their motives
parents thinking about values beyond career
not_for: someone looking for comfort rather than critique
research_note: Manas Piyush vol. 7 read at Uttar doha 99.

verified_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Uttar Kand doha 108: the first of the two dohas Manas Piyush prints together as ॥108 (ख)॥, Gita Press numbering. Our id says '104 doha 3': off by four.
attribution_note: The Brahmin guru (Kakbhushundi's teacher in his Ujjain life) praying to Shiva, as stated.
translation_note: Accurate. The companion doha goes on: 'Shankara, kind to the lowly, be gracious to him now, so that the curse may become a blessing in a short time.'
context: In an earlier life Kakbhushundi, a proud Shiva devotee in Ujjain, would not rise when his gentle guru entered Shiva's temple. A voice from the sky (Shiva) cursed him to be born a serpent for a thousand lives. The guru, horrified, sang the Rudrashtakam and then made this plea for his rude student. Shiva softened the curse, and devotion survived through all those births.

key_terms.sense: in the grip of maya, illusion

core_teaching: The wronged teacher pleads for the one who wronged him: the student acted from illusion and deserves pity, not wrath. Here mercy flows from the injured party.

commentaries.gist: Hanuman and the Vedas say the same to Ram: souls wander deluded by your maya. The dull student deserves compassion, not anger. Each epithet (Prabhu, ocean of mercy, Bhagavan, kind to the lowly) names a power to forgive.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ram Vallabhasharan, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: A servant shouldn't overturn his master's order outright, so the guru asks Shiva, who is able, to keep his word yet make the curse end in the student's good soon, rather than after untold ages.
Shiva's anger is calmed by the Brahmin's devotion (a rasa figure called samahita).

practical_reading: Used to model praying or speaking up for someone who hurt you, seeing their wrong as confusion rather than wickedness, without excusing it.
misreadings: Not a claim that the wrong didn't matter; the guru accepts that a curse is deserved and asks that it be softened.
Not an obligation on victims to plead for those who harmed them.
cautions: The context includes a curse of a thousand serpent births; keep that out of readings for anxious or guilt-prone readers.
speaks_to: forgiving a student, child or junior who disrespected you
praying for someone who wronged you
not_for: victims of serious harm, who may hear pressure to plead for their abuser
research_note: Manas Piyush vol. 7 read at Uttar doha 108.

verified_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Uttar Kand doha 110, chaupai 1 (Manas Piyush half-lines 1-2), Gita Press numbering. Our id says doha 106: off by four.
attribution_note: Kakbhushundi to Garuda, as stated.
translation_note: Accurate. Manas Piyush explains the 'thorn' as lasting remorse at having insulted such a gentle guru.
context: After Shiva's curse, softened at the guru's plea, Kakbhushundi passes through many births as animals, gods and humans, keeping up his devotion to Ram. The one pain that never fades is the memory of his teacher's gentleness, which he had insulted. In his final birth he is born a Brahmin and as a boy plays at Ram's deeds. Then comes the episode with the sage Lomash.

key_terms.sense: I kept up worship of Ram

core_teaching: Through many lives Kakbhushundi held to his devotion, yet the ache of having wronged a gentle teacher never left him. The memory of someone's kindness can be the deepest remorse.

commentaries.gist: The 'one thorn' is lasting remorse: he never forgot how gravely he had insulted his gentle guru.
Order of births: first a thousand serpent lives for the curse, then divine bodies to enjoy past merit, then human births of rising station, and finally a Brahmin body.
His right to worship continued in every body.

commentaries.who: Baijnath, earlier note in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: Shows the principle that mental merit counts but mental sin does not: while his disrespect stayed in thought he was not punished, and only the open insult brought the curse.

practical_reading: Used for regret that lasts: the harm we did to someone who was only kind to us stays with us. Teachers treat it as conscience to keep, not self-punishment.
misreadings: Not 'regret forever'; in the story it sits alongside lasting devotion and leads to humility.
cautions: Assumes many rebirths; a reader carrying heavy guilt may hear it as 'this will never leave you'.
speaks_to: regret over hurting a teacher, parent or mentor
remembering someone's gentleness after they're gone
not_for: someone already crushed by guilt or with intrusive self-blame
research_note: Manas Piyush vol. 7 read at Uttar doha 110.

verified_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Uttar Kand doha 111, chaupai 8 (Manas Piyush half-lines 15-16), Gita Press numbering. Our id says doha 107: off by four.
attribution_note: Kakbhushundi to Garuda (addressed as 'प्रभु'), as stated.
translation_note: Accurate. Manas Piyush records variants 'ज्ञानिहु' (even the wise) and 'चंदनहु' (even sandal), which strengthen the 'even' in our translation.
context: In his last human birth young Kakbhushundi goes to the sage Lomash. Lomash teaches the formless Brahman, but the boy keeps pressing for devotion to the embodied Ram and argues back again and again. The sage's anger shows on his face, and Kakbhushundi admits here that relentless disrespect angers even the wise. Lomash finally curses him to become a crow, which he accepts calmly.

key_terms.sense: in the hearts of the wise

core_teaching: Even the calmest person will flare up under relentless provocation, as sandalwood ignites if rubbed hard enough. The speaker takes responsibility for having been the friction.

commentaries.gist: The text says 'jnani' (the learned), not 'sant': anger arose in a man of knowledge, and true devotee-saints, alike in praise and blame, don't flare up. Lomash is the sandal, and the back-and-forth argument the friction.
The wise are cool like sandal, but as fire lies hidden in sandal, anger lies subtly in them, held down by discipline. Ordinary rubbing won't light it, only extreme friction.

commentaries.who: Vinayak Rao's tika, citing Mahabharata Vana Parva
commentaries.gist: Neither constant anger nor constant forgiveness is always best, and the wise do not praise forgiving every time. Some anger at extreme provocation is understandable.

practical_reading: Used two ways: to own one's part when one has provoked someone patient, and to forgive oneself or others for snapping after long strain.
misreadings: Not a licence to keep pushing someone until they break.
Not a defence of rage; the speaker is admitting his own fault.
speaks_to: a patient person who finally lost their temper
owning one's part in a conflict
not_for: someone being harmed by another's anger, who may hear it as 'you provoked it'
research_note: Manas Piyush vol. 7 read at Uttar doha 111.

verified_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Uttar Kand doha 112 (second of the pair printed as ॥112॥), Gita Press / Manas Piyush. Our ref says 108: off by four.
attribution_note: Shiva to Uma, as stated. Manas Piyush notes that Kakbhushundi's words end at 'flew off joyfully', and this doha is Shiva's.
translation_note: Accurate.
context: Lomash curses Kakbhushundi, who instantly becomes a crow. He bows at the sage's feet, remembers Ram and flies away happy, with no fear or bitterness. Shiva explains why. Lomash then repents, calls him back and blesses him with devotion and the Ram story.

key_terms.sense: free of desire, pride and anger
see the world full of their own Lord

core_teaching: One who sees their Beloved everywhere has no one left to fight. That is why Kakbhushundi can be cursed and still leave in joy.

commentaries.gist: 'Seeing the world full of the Lord': seeing every being as Ram's form, or Ram as the inner mover of all. Either way no room is left for fear or enmity. Compares Bhagavata 11.29 and Isha Upanishad 6.

commentaries.who: Ram Shankar Sharan, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: He bows at the cursing sage's feet because Shiva had taught him to treat a saint as the Infinite. He remembers Ram because remembrance makes the hard easy.

commentaries.who: Manas Piyush compiler's note (on the curse)
commentaries.gist: He leaves joyful and not humbled. He also doesn't change his form of worship out of fear of the curse: he stays devoted to Ram of the Raghu line, not to the formless the sage preached.

practical_reading: Used to show freedom from resentment: if you can see the sacred in the person who wronged you, there's nothing left to fight over.
misreadings: Not a requirement to accept mistreatment silently.
cautions: In context this follows an unjust curse; don't present it as 'accept injustice cheerfully' to someone being wronged now.
not_for: someone facing ongoing injustice who needs to resist it
research_note: Manas Piyush vol. 7 read at Uttar doha 112.

verified_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Uttar Kand doha 120, chaupais 1-2 (Manas Piyush half-lines 1-4), Gita Press numbering. Our id says doha 116: off by four.
attribution_note: Kakbhushundi to Garuda, as stated.
translation_note: Accurate.
context: Garuda asked why knowledge and devotion differ. Kakbhushundi has just finished the long 'lamp of knowledge' allegory: knowledge is a lamp, hard to light and easily blown out by maya's winds. Now he turns to devotion as a wish-fulfilling gem that shines by itself and that greed, delusion and maya cannot touch.

key_terms.sense: lamp, ghee and wick: the apparatus a lamp needs

core_teaching: Knowledge is a lamp that needs fuel and can be blown out. Devotion is a jewel that shines on its own, day and night, and no wind of greed can put it out.

commentaries.gist: Garuda asked to have it explained, and 'I have explained' closes the knowledge section. 'Listen' opens the next.

Knowledge and devotion share one conclusion and differ in power. A gem takes the colour of what holds it, as the mind settles once freed of attachment. A chintamani grants every wish, so devotion to Ram grants everything.
The lamp of knowledge can be obstructed, while the gem of devotion can't be: it is unbroken, ageless, priceless and always shining.
A pun on 'बुझाई': 'I explained' knowledge, and also 'I showed how the lamp gets blown out'.

practical_reading: Teachers use the contrast for steadiness: understanding can flicker under stress, but love and trust can keep shining when the mind is shaken.
misreadings: Not anti-intellectual; the commentary says knowledge and devotion reach the same end.
speaks_to: people who feel their understanding keeps slipping
research_note: Manas Piyush vol. 7 read at Uttar doha 120.

verified_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Uttar Kand doha 120, chaupai 9 (Manas Piyush half-lines 17-18), Gita Press numbering. Our id says doha 116: off by four.
attribution_note: Kakbhushundi to Garuda, as stated.
translation_note: Accurate.
context: Just before this Kakbhushundi says, 'My faith is that Ram's servant is greater than Ram.' These two images explain why: the sea's water reaches the land only through clouds, and the sandal tree's scent spreads only on the breeze. The doha that follows says saints churn devotion's sweetness from the ocean of Brahman.

key_terms.sense: the steady good are the clouds

core_teaching: The divine is like the sea or the sandal tree, but good people are the clouds and breeze that carry its sweetness to everyone. No one gains devotion without them.

commentaries.gist: Scripture says no one equals Ram, but a saint's tested experience also counts. Kakbhushundi states his own conviction that the servant is greater. He also separates 'dasa' (wholly given over) from 'sevaka' (one who serves but could leave).

The sea is deep, fixed, out of reach and salty; clouds draw out sweet water and rain it everywhere. So saints carry Ram's glory to all. Compare Bal Kand 36, where scripture is the ocean and saints the clouds.

practical_reading: Used to honour the people who brought the sacred, or simply goodness, within reach: a grandparent, a teacher, a friend. They are the breeze that carried the scent.
misreadings: Not literally that humans outrank God; it is about how grace reaches people.
speaks_to: gratitude to a mentor, grandparent or teacher
those who serve as carriers of goodness
research_note: Manas Piyush vol. 7 read at Uttar doha 120.

verified_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Uttar Kand doha 121, chaupai 6 (Manas Piyush half-lines 11-12), Gita Press numbering. Our id says doha 117: off by four.
attribution_note: Kakbhushundi to Garuda, answering Garuda's seven questions (the first: which body is best), as stated.
translation_note: Accurate. 'मंद मंदतर' means dull and duller still. Manas Piyush notes a variant 'जिमि' for 'ते'. 'काँच किरिच' is a shard of glass (Ramayan Pradip: iron dross).
context: Garuda has asked seven questions. To the first, which body is best, Kakbhushundi answers that the human body is, sought even by moving and unmoving beings, because it can reach liberation and devotion. These lines describe those who waste it. Next come the answers on the greatest sorrow and joy.

key_terms.sense: the philosopher's stone (turns iron to gold)

core_teaching: Spending a rare human life only on passing pleasures is like throwing away a philosopher's stone for a shard of glass.

commentaries.gist: Those who don't worship are dull. Those who also chase pleasures are duller still. Worship is the philosopher's stone and pleasures the shard of glass.
They become ever duller and slide toward animal and even inert births.
Seeking happiness, such a person chases the mere appearance of it through great hardship. Their mind clouds further each day until return seems impossible.

practical_reading: Used as a wake-up line about priorities: don't trade what is precious (time, love, the chance to grow) for what glitters briefly.
misreadings: Not contempt for ordinary enjoyment; it is about trading the precious for the trivial.
cautions: Harsh judgement ('dull and duller'); could shame someone in addiction or depression.
not_for: someone in addiction recovery who needs compassion
a reader with low self-worth
research_note: Manas Piyush vol. 7 read at Uttar doha 121.

verified_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Uttar Kand doha 121, chaupai 7 (Manas Piyush half-lines 13-14), Gita Press numbering. Our id says doha 117: off by four.
attribution_note: Kakbhushundi to Garuda, as stated.
translation_note: Accurate. 'दरिद्र' is poverty, want. The next line (not in our text) adds that saints suffer for others' good and the wicked suffer just to cause others pain.
context: These are Kakbhushundi's answers to Garuda's second, third and fourth questions: the greatest sorrow (poverty), the greatest joy (meeting the good), and the nature of saints (doing good in word, thought and deed). He goes on to the wicked, then the highest virtue and worst sin, then the diseases of the mind.
core_teaching: Want is the hardest sorrow in this world and good company the greatest joy, and doing good in word, mind and body is simply what good people are like.

commentaries.gist: Many sorrows exist, but none like poverty: even a wife may leave the destitute. Kakbhushundi knew it, having gone to Ujjain poor in a famine. Cites sayings that a forest life beats poverty among relatives.
In the world even the smallest comfort costs money, so the poor suffer most. But some penniless renunciants are deeply happy. The real poverty is delusion ('moha daridra').

Cold without clothes and hunger without food make one forget every other pain. Meeting saints is the greatest joy: other joys leave craving and end in pain, while this one is whole and good to the end.

commentaries.who: Ram Shankar Sharan, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: Kakbhushundi speaks from experience: meeting one great saint brought him to this highest joy.

practical_reading: Used to take material hardship seriously, without spiritualising it away, and to treasure good company as the best thing life offers.
misreadings: Not a claim that poor people can't be happy (Vijayanand Tripathi rejects that).
Not a reason to look down on the poor.
cautions: For a reader in financial hardship, 'no sorrow like poverty' can validate or deepen despair; pair with the joy-of-good-company half.
speaks_to: loneliness and the value of good friends
not_for: someone in acute financial crisis, unless the reading is careful and practical
research_note: Manas Piyush vol. 7 read at Uttar doha 121.

verified_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Uttar Kand doha 121, chaupai 11 (Manas Piyush half-lines 21-22), Gita Press numbering. Our id says doha 117: off by four.
attribution_note: Kakbhushundi to Garuda, as stated.
translation_note: Accurate. 'गरीसा' (heavy as a mountain-king) in 'न अघ गरीसा': no sin as heavy as a mountain like slander. Manas Piyush also reads 'गिरीसा'.
context: Just before this: the rise of the wicked brings the world misery, like the ill-omened comet Ketu. Here the rise of the good brings joy, and the answers on the highest virtue and the worst sin follow. Right after come the rebirths of slanderers (as frogs, crows, bats), and then the diseases of the mind.

key_terms.sense: the rise, prosperity of the good

core_teaching: When good people rise, everyone gains, as the sun and moon serve the whole world. Non-harm is the highest duty, and slandering others the heaviest wrong.

commentaries.gist: In power the wicked hurt the world; the rise of the good benefits all. Ahimsa, harming no creature, roots all yamas and niyamas. Slander joins lying to harm: destroying a reputation is like killing many times over.

commentaries.who: Vijayanand Tripathi on nindā vs parivāda
commentaries.gist: Telling a true fault is parivada, and inventing one is ninda. Either becomes grave when done to wound, while pointing out a fault to help someone improve is not condemned.

commentaries.who: Ram Shankar Sharan, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: Garuda asked which merit the Veda calls highest, and the answer matches his words: 'the Veda knows ahimsa as the highest dharma'.

practical_reading: Used to rank wrongs plainly: gossip and character assassination are not small sins. Celebrate the success of good people, because it lifts everyone.
misreadings: Not a ban on honest criticism meant to help someone improve (the commentary makes this distinction).
cautions: The very next lines describe slanderers reborn as frogs and crows; keep that out of readings.
not_for: someone who has been slandered and needs comfort, not a lecture
research_note: Manas Piyush vol. 7 read at Uttar doha 121.

verified_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Uttar Kand doha 121, chaupai 15 (Manas Piyush half-lines 29-30), Gita Press numbering. Our id says doha 117: off by four.
attribution_note: Kakbhushundi to Garuda, answering Garuda's seventh question on the 'diseases of the mind', as stated.
translation_note: Accurate. Vata, kapha and pitta are the three Ayurvedic humours (wind, phlegm, bile). Our 'wind', 'phlegm' and 'bile' are fine. The next line says that when all three combine the result is sannipata, a dangerous delirious fever.
context: This answers Garuda's last and most important question, what the diseases of the mind are. It opens an extended medical allegory: delusion is the root, desire, greed and anger are the three humours, and envy, possessiveness and the rest are skin and throat diseases. The cure comes after: Ram's grace, a true teacher as physician, and devotion as the medicine.
core_teaching: Delusion is the root disease of the mind. From it come desire, greed and anger, which, like the body's three humours out of balance, burn and choke us, and together become a delirious fever.

commentaries.gist: Bodily diseases don't strike everyone, but mental ones afflict all people in some measure. That is why the verse says 'all people' suffer from them.

Mental diseases are rooted in delusion, bodily ones in 'prajnaparadha' (failed judgement, itself ignorance). Vata, pitta and kapha hold the body and cause disease only when unbalanced; desire, anger and greed do the same in the mind.
Desire is vata because vata alone moves and carries the other two wherever it goes, just as desire leads anger and greed.
Just as the three humours together make sannipata, desire, anger and greed together make a great sinner.

practical_reading: A favourite text for a 'psychology of the Manas': treat craving, greed and anger as states that can be diagnosed and treated, not as fixed identity. Teachers like the medical framing because it removes shame.
misreadings: Not a statement about clinical mental illness; 'manas rog' here means moral and emotional afflictions, not depression or anxiety disorders.
Not medical advice.
cautions: Don't use it to suggest that a reader's diagnosed mental illness comes from desire, greed or anger.
speaks_to: people drawn to Ayurveda and psychology
not_for: someone with a mental health condition who may hear it as moral blame
research_note: Manas Piyush vol. 7 read at Uttar doha 121.

verified_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Uttar Kand doha 121, chaupai 17 (Manas Piyush half-lines 33-34), Gita Press numbering. Our id says doha 117: off by four.
attribution_note: Kakbhushundi to Garuda, as stated.
translation_note: Broadly right. 'गरह' is disputed in Manas Piyush. Readings include goitre or throat swelling (Baijnath), scrofula, chronic dysentery (Ramayan Pradip), gout (Panjabi ji), and 'graha', a seizure by spirits or planets (Hindi Shabdasagar, Vijayanand Tripathi). Our 'throat ailments' follows the majority. 'छई' is consumption (tuberculosis) and 'कुष्ट' leprosy.
context: This continues the 'diseases of the mind' allegory. Just before: the endless desires are countless kinds of colic. Just after: pride, deceit, hypocrisy and the like are further diseases, and the doha that follows says one disease can kill and these are many, so how can anyone find peace? The cure comes next.

key_terms.sense: elation and dejection as throat disease (or 'seizures')
burning at others' happiness is consumption

core_teaching: Possessiveness, envy, mood swings and the burn of others' happiness are diseases that eat at us from within, each matched to a physical illness.

commentaries.gist: Explains each disease medically. Ringworm is a red, itchy circle (counted among the minor kushthas). Scabies is many small itching, burning pustules. The difference is that ringworm forms a ring and scabies burns.

commentaries.who: Several commentators on 'गरह', in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: Most read it as a throat disease such as goitre (Baijnath: from vata-kapha and bad water). Others read graha (possession, seizures), dysentery or gout. Vijayanand Tripathi lists the many grahas of Madhava Nidana.

practical_reading: Used as a self-check list: possessiveness itches, envy burns, mood swings choke, and resentment of others' happiness wastes you. Each is named so it can be treated.
misreadings: Not a statement about people with these physical diseases; the diseases are metaphors.
cautions: Uses leprosy, tuberculosis and skin disease as images of moral fault; avoid with readers who have or care for someone with these illnesses, and avoid stigmatising language.
not_for: readers with chronic illness, especially skin disease, TB or leprosy
someone in a depressive low ('dejection as disease' may shame)
research_note: Manas Piyush vol. 7 read at Uttar doha 121.

verified_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Uttar Kand doha 125 (second doha of the pair printed as ॥125॥), Gita Press / Manas Piyush. Our ref says 121: off by four.
attribution_note: Shiva to Girija (Parvati), as stated.
translation_note: Accurate.
context: Garuda, his doubts gone, bows at Kakbhushundi's feet with love and returns to Vaikuntha with Ram in his heart. This doha is where Shiva closes the whole Garuda-Kakbhushundi frame. Then he tells Parvati how blessed she is to have heard the story.
core_teaching: The company of good, wise people is the greatest gain, and it comes as grace, not as something we simply arrange.

commentaries.gist: This closes the frame begun when Garuda went to Kakbhushundi. Garuda now bows to him as to a guru, though he came as king of birds and was honoured as one. His doubt is gone, so his mind is steady.

commentaries.who: Manas Piyush footnote, citing Bhagavata Mahatmya 2.76
commentaries.gist: Satsang comes when merit gathered over many births ripens. It dispels the darkness of delusion and pride born of ignorance, and discernment dawns.
'Keeping Raghubir in his heart' means Garuda now sees Ram as the supreme Self, where before he thought the lord of Vaikuntha the highest.

practical_reading: Used to treasure the good people in one's life as gifts, not achievements, and to be grateful for meeting the right person at the right time.
misreadings: Not a reason to wait passively for good company; elsewhere the text urges seeking it out.
speaks_to: gratitude for a mentor or friend
loneliness and the longing for good company
not_for: someone isolated, who may hear 'you lack grace'
research_note: Manas Piyush vol. 7 read at Uttar doha 125.

verified_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Uttar Kand doha 130, chaupai 3 (Manas Piyush half-lines 5-6), Gita Press numbering. Our id says doha 126: off by four.
attribution_note: Manas Piyush says plainly that from here on these are Tulsidas's own words, as he closes his own frame of the dialogue. So the speaker is Tulsidas and the listener the reader (his own mind). Our 'Shiva / Tulsidas → Parvati / the reader' should be simplified to Tulsidas → the reader.
translation_note: Accurate. Manas Piyush reads 'जज्ञ' and 'ब्रत' (garbled in its OCR).
context: Each frame has closed: Shiva-Parvati, Yajnavalkya-Bharadwaj, Kakbhushundi-Garuda. Tulsidas now speaks in his own voice to sum up the work. He says that in the Kali age the one means left is remembering, singing and hearing of Ram, and that his own mind found peace this way. The closing prayers and the phalashruti follow.

key_terms.sense: the Kali age, the present dark age

core_teaching: In a hard age, when elaborate disciplines are out of reach, the simplest means are enough: remember Ram, sing of him and keep hearing his story.

commentaries.gist: Tulsidas now closes his own dialogue. In Kali, short lives, weak minds, illness and scarce means make yoga, sacrifice, ritual japa, tapas and vows impractical. Cites Bhagavata 1.1.10 and 1.2.14: hear, sing, meditate on and worship the Lord.

No one can change the season, but in summer one can shelter with khus screens and fans. Remembering Ram is such a shelter in the scorching age of Kali, where living among the wicked makes dharma hard to keep.
Fit the practice to the situation: alone, remember; with good company, sing together; with a good speaker, listen. Say the name aloud, since silent remembrance alone is not enough in this age.

practical_reading: Used to make practice light and possible in a busy life: a name remembered, a song, a story heard is enough to begin.
misreadings: Not a dismissal of ethics or of other paths; it is about what is feasible.
cautions: Devotional and Ram-specific; for a non-devotional reader, frame it as simple practices that keep the mind steady.
speaks_to: people with no time for elaborate practice
not_for: readers who want a philosophical argument
research_note: Manas Piyush vol. 7 read at Uttar doha 130.

verified_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Uttar Kand doha 130 (ka), Gita Press / Manas Piyush. Our ref says 126: off by four.
attribution_note: Tulsidas to Ram, as stated.
translation_note: Accurate. 'भव भीर' is the distress or crush of worldly existence (the round of birth and death), glossed in Manas Piyush as 'bhava-sankat'. 'Heavy fear of the world' is acceptable.
context: Tulsidas has said his own mind found peace in Ram's story. As the poem closes he makes two last prayers in doha form. This is the first: he is the poorest of the poor and Ram the greatest friend of the poor, so let Ram remove his burden. The second asks that Ram be as dear to him as a lover is to the lustful and money to the greedy.

key_terms.sense: friend and benefactor of the lowly
the grievous crush of worldly existence

core_teaching: Tulsidas stakes his whole claim on need, not merit: I am as helpless as anyone could be, and you are as kind to the helpless as anyone could be, so the match is made.

commentaries.who: Manas Piyush compiler's note, citing Vinaya Patrika 242
commentaries.gist: The same pairing runs through Vinaya Patrika: none is as poor as I, no friend of the poor like you; I am crooked and you remove crookedness; I am orphaned and you are the friend of orphans.

Of a work's four anubandhas, this doha states the relationship: a lowly devotee seeking refuge with the friend of the lowly. Only one free of becoming can rescue others from it, and even Brahma admits he is caught.
Why claim only this relation and not master-servant or father-son? Because 'I can do no service; my only trust is your mercy'.

practical_reading: A prayer for low moments: you don't have to be worthy to ask. Your need itself is the qualification.
misreadings: Not self-hatred; it is humility used as a claim on grace.
speaks_to: praying when you have nothing to offer
not_for: someone with very low self-worth who might take 'none as poor as I' literally
research_note: Manas Piyush vol. 7 read at Uttar doha 130.

verified_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Uttar Kand doha 130 (kha), Gita Press / Manas Piyush. The last doha of the poem (only closing Sanskrit shlokas follow). Our ref says 126: off by four.
attribution_note: Tulsidas to Ram, as stated.
translation_note: Accurate. Pande ji, in Manas Piyush, takes the direct address 'Raghunath ... Ram' to mean that Ram became visible to Tulsidas at the poem's end.
context: This is the last doha of the Manas, the second of Tulsidas's two closing prayers. Only the closing Sanskrit shlokas and the phalashruti follow. It borrows the two strongest human cravings as the measure of the love he asks for.

key_terms.sense: as a woman is dear to a lustful man
as money is dear to a greedy man

core_teaching: Tulsidas asks to love God with the same effortless, all-consuming pull that lust and greed exert, turning the strongest cravings into the measure of devotion.

commentaries.gist: Compare Vinaya Patrika 269, with five such loves (water to fish, wealth to the greedy, lover to lover...). The craving lover needs no technique: the beloved fills his mind sleeping and waking, and he gives up everything.

commentaries.who: Manas Piyush compiler's note on Tulsidas's life
commentaries.gist: Cites the tradition (Mul Charit) that Tulsidas himself knew this attachment to his wife before renunciation, as Bilvamangala did. He prays that the same intensity now turn toward Ram.
The direct address suggests Ram appeared to Tulsidas at the end of the work.

practical_reading: Teachers use it to say: you already know how to love intensely, so point that capacity at what is highest. It is a frank, unpious picture of devotion.
misreadings: Not an endorsement of lust or greed; they are measures of intensity.
Not a view of women as objects, though the gendered image reflects its era.
cautions: The image is gendered (a woman as the object of a lustful man). Some readers will find it jarring; consider a gender-neutral paraphrase ('as a lover is to one who desires').
speaks_to: wanting a deeper, more natural devotion
not_for: readers sensitive to gendered imagery, without reframing
someone struggling with addiction (craving as a model may be unhelpful)
research_note: Manas Piyush vol. 7 read at Uttar doha 130.
